events.text: A baby is coming in the house next to yours, and it has been coming since noon. The midwife has sent everyone out of the yard. At dusk you go to shut the brushwood gate and find it already occupied. Something is standing there: the body of a roe deer covered in small scales that catch the lamplight in five colours, a short single horn on its forehead with a soft rounded tip, and pale flames curling round its hooves that do not scorch the straw. It is standing very still, one forefoot raised. An ant road runs across the threshold stone, and it is waiting for the ants to finish. The old women of the village say that when this beast comes to a birth, someone must tie a ribbon to its horn.
events.arc: The Beast That Would Not Step

choices.text: Tie a ribbon round its horn, as the old women say

effects.log: You have nothing but the faded red ribbon off your own sewing basket. You hold it up, and the beast lowers its head for you, slowly, the way a tired ox lowers its head for the yoke, and you tie it round the horn in a double knot. The tip of the horn is warm and soft, like the inside of a wrist. It stays at the gate two nights, never once stepping on the ant road, and on the morning the child is born it is gone. Your ribbon went with it.

choices.text: Throw a stone at it, to drive it from the gate

effects.log: You throw it hard, at the flank. The stone stops in the air a hand's width from the scales, hangs there, and drops into the dust. Not a blade of the weeds by the gate is bent. The beast turns its head and looks at you, and there is nothing in its look at all: no anger, no fear. Only patience. You have never felt so small in your life. It stays two nights. You do not go near the gate again until it has gone.

choices.text: Kneel by the gate and wait with it for the last ant

effects.log: You kneel in the dust beside it. The ants go by, one and then another, carrying crumbs of rice from somebody's dropped bowl. It takes until full dark. When the last ant has crossed, the beast sets its forefoot down, carefully, on the bare stone, and breathes out through its nose, and you realise you have been holding your breath too. It stays two nights. The child next door is born on the second, healthy and very quiet.

events.text: Autumn, and the threshing yard is swept and empty at dawn. In the middle of it stands a colt you have never seen: small, slender, grey-gold, with legs like a young roe deer's and a lump on its forehead like a bud that has not opened. It is eating the chestnuts that fell in the night, only the fallen ones. It walks round the one green weed growing in the crack of the yard stone as if the weed were a sleeping baby. Nobody else is awake.
events.arc: The Beast That Would Not Step

choices.text: Fetch the bridle from the cowshed

effects.log: You come back with the old rope bridle dragging behind you. The colt looks at the bridle, and at you, and lowers its head so that you can put it on, because you so obviously want to. You lead it once round the threshing yard, proud as a general. Then you take the bridle off again, because it is wrong, somehow, and you do not know why. When you look up from coiling the rope it is gone.

choices.text: Gather chestnuts and share them with it

effects.log: You pick up fallen chestnuts with it until your fingers are prickled red and you have a heap. You eat one; it eats one. It does not take any you have peeled for yourself. When the sun comes over the ridge it touches its soft nose to your forehead, once, warm as bread, and walks off up the hill between the furrows without stepping on a single stalk.

choices.text: Run and wake the whole village

effects.log: You run, shouting, and bang on every gate, and by the time the grown-ups come out in their sleeping clothes the threshing yard is empty except for chestnut husks. Everybody laughs. The old man of the house cuffs you. But the old woman from the end house looks at the little weed in the crack of the yard stone, standing straight, and at the hoofprints that go round it in a careful circle, and she does not laugh at all. (-2 health)

events.text: An alchemists' sect has posted a bounty at every inn on the river road: a hundred taels for the horn of a five-coloured horned beast, alive or otherwise. {npc}, a bounty hunter you have shared a fire with, tracked it to a ford and asked you along for the strength. Now it is the third day. You have fought the beast on the riverbank from dawn to dark three times over, and it has never once struck back. It is behind you. It is on the water. It is standing exactly where your sword was not. Your arms are lead. Its scales do not have a mark on them. {npc} and the sect's hunters are coming up the bank with ropes.
events.arc: The Beast That Would Not Step

choices.text: Keep fighting until it lets you cut it

effects.log: On the third evening it stops moving. It simply stands and lets your blade come. The cut opens along its shoulder, and closes, as you watch, like water closing over a stone. There is no blood on your sword. There is only the beast, looking at you with nothing in its eyes but a great tiredness, and then it walks out across the river on the surface of the water. {npc} says you are the only one who ever touched it. You cannot meet anyone's eyes for a month.

choices.text: Lay down your sword and sit on the bank

effects.log: You put your sword on the stones and sit down, because there is nothing else to do with your body. After a long while the beast comes and lies down too, an arm's length off, its legs folded under it like a deer's. You sit together until the moon comes up. {npc} arrives with the hunters, stares at the two of you, and sits down as well, very slowly, as if not sure it is allowed. In the morning only the hunters are on the bank.

choices.text: Turn round and hold the ford against the hunters

ok.log: You turn your back on the beast and face your own side. "Nobody crosses," you say, and nobody does: you hold the ford until full dark, and when the last hunter limps off swearing at you, you look round and the beast is standing on the river behind you, a hand above the water, watching you as if you had done something astonishing. {npc} goes with the hunters. You will not get that bounty, or any other on that road, again.

fail.log: You turn your back on the beast and face the hunters and there are too many of them. They put you on the stones. But the time it took them was all the beast needed: when they look up it is gone across the water, and the ropes are slack in their hands. {npc} binds your head afterward and calls you an idiot, gently. (-14 health)

events.text: A lord who rules three provinces by the sword has invited you to his autumn hunt in the west, because a power that heaven listens to is good to have at one's side, and good to be seen with. On the second day the beaters bring in something nobody can name: the body of a roe deer in small dragon scales gone dull with dust, a single short horn with a soft tip, cloven hooves, a tufted tail like an ox's. Its right foreleg is broken. A carter caught it and thought it unlucky and gave it to the forester, and the forester has brought it to the lord in a cart. The lord's omen-readers are arguing. And at the back of the crowd an old scholar has seen the faded embroidered ribbon still knotted round its horn, and has turned back a sleeve to wipe his face, and is weeping into it.
events.arc: The Beast That Would Not Step

choices.text: Heal its leg and take it out of the lord's hands

effects.log: You walk to the cart without asking and put your hands on the broken leg and pour your qi into the bone until it knits. The lord's guards draw. You look at them and they put their swords away again. You lift the beast down. It stands, tests the leg, and touches its horn to your sleeve, very lightly. Then it walks out of the lord's camp and nobody stops it. The lord smiles at you all through dinner and never invites you again, and you know exactly what that smile means.

choices.text: Tell the lord it is an omen of his glory, and let him keep it

effects.log: "It has come for you," you tell the lord, because it is what he wants and you want the lord's goodwill. He is delighted. The beast is put in a pen of gilded timber at the centre of his camp. The old scholar looks at you across the crowd for a long moment and then turns away, and you hear later that he went home and burned his brushes and wrote nothing more. You will not forget his face.

choices.text: End the lord's war in a day, so it can be let go into a peace

ok.log: "It cannot live anywhere else," you tell the lord, "so make it a peace." You ride out that night to his enemy's camp alone and come back at dawn with a truce sealed in red wax, and the lord, who cannot refuse a gift from a power like you in front of his own army, signs it. The beast is carried to the edge of the woods and set down. It walks into the trees on three legs and then, suddenly, on four. The old scholar laughs out loud, and then weeps again.

fail.log: You try to end the war in a day and it takes a season, and costs you a wound you will carry for years, and the lord hates every hour of it. But it ends. On the day the truce is sealed you open the beast's pen with your own hands, and it limps out into the frost and goes. (-18 health)

events.text: A hall of the Jade court, its floor a single cloud. The court is asking a question it asks once in a thousand years, and has asked you to answer it, because you came up from the world below recently enough to remember it. In the middle of the hall, standing on the cloud as if on a meadow it is afraid to bruise, is a beast like a roe deer covered in scales of five colours, a short horn on its brow with a soft tip, pale flames round its hooves. Below the cloud floor the world can be seen: two armies on a plain, a burning town, a sect hall where someone is being beaten. "Should it go down," the presiding immortal asks, "in an age like this one?"
events.arc: The Beast That Would Not Step

choices.text: Say it should go down: the age needs it most when it is worst

effects.log: "If it only comes when the age is good," you say, "it only comes when nobody needs it." The hall murmurs. The beast lifts its head and looks at you, and for a moment you see your own village below, on the morning after some war, and a child standing in a doorway. The presiding immortal writes something. The beast steps off the edge of the cloud and goes down, and the hall is quieter without it.

choices.text: Say it must wait above until the age is fit for it

effects.log: "They will hunt it," you say. "They will break its legs and put it in a cage and say it came for them. I have seen it." Nobody in the hall argues; several of them have seen it too. The beast lowers its head. It does not go down. When you leave the hall it is lying on the cloud with its chin on its forelegs, looking through the floor at the world, waiting, as it has waited before.

choices.text: Say you will go down first, and make the age fit for it

ok.log: "Give me a hundred years," you say. The court laughs, and then sees that you mean it, and stops laughing. The presiding immortal writes your name on a slip of jade and gives it to the beast, which takes it gently in its mouth. You go down to the world with the cold of that hall still in your sleeves, and the first war you end, you end without killing anyone, because something on a cloud is watching how you do it.

fail.log: "Give me a hundred years," you say, and your voice cracks on it, and a few of the older immortals smile in a way that is not kind. But the beast takes a step toward you on the cloud, and that is enough: the court writes your promise down. You find out what a hundred years of keeping it costs. (-8 health)

events.text: {npc}, a recorder of the Jade court with ink on every finger, finds you on a terrace of cloud a few years after the court asked its question. "The beast keeps a ledger," {npc} says, "not of what anyone did to it. Of every blade of grass it has ever bent. It is very short. It asked whether you would read it, since you answered for it."
events.arc: The Beast That Would Not Step

choices.text: Read the ledger

effects.log: Four lines in a thousand years: a stalk of barley, a beetle on a dark road, a fawn frightened into a ravine, a hunter's hand bruised when it pulled free of a snare. Each with a date, and beside each, in a different ink, what was done to mend it. You give the ledger back and go to your own rooms and sit for a long time, trying to remember how many lines your own would have.

choices.text: Tell {npc} that it is not yours to read

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, as if this were also the answer the beast expected, and tucks the ledger away. "It said you might say that," {npc} admits. "It said that was the answer it would have given."

events.text: The child born in the house next door the night the beast stood at the gate is a small child now, and reads. Nobody taught the child; the child simply looked at the almanac on the wall long enough and then began to read it aloud. The village says it is the ribbon. The child's family is too poor for a teacher, and the village school master has said the child asks too many questions to be any good.

choices.text: Teach the child what little you know

effects.log: You know perhaps two hundred characters. The child learns them all in a month and then starts teaching them back to you, better. You sit under the persimmon tree in the evenings and are corrected. It is the best schooling you have ever had.

choices.text: Take the child to the temple, where the monks have books

effects.log: The old monk at the hill temple hears the child read three lines of a sutra and puts down his tea. "Who taught this one?" "Nobody," you say. The monk looks at the child for a long time and then says the child may come every morning, and sweep, and read whatever is not locked.

choices.text: Leave it: the child is not yours to raise

effects.log: You leave it. Every evening you hear the child reading the almanac aloud through the fence, the same pages over and over, because there is nothing else in the house to read. One evening the reading stops, and does not start again, and you find you miss it more than you expected.

events.text: The child of the ribbon is grown, a teacher of village children in a schoolroom with a leaking roof, and the magistrate's office has sent word that the school is to close: the teacher has been teaching the children of butchers and slaves alongside the children of the clerks. The teacher has come to ask your advice, and is very calm about it, the way the beast was calm at the gate.

choices.text: Help them keep the school open, whatever it costs

ok.log: You go with the teacher to the magistrate and speak until the magistrate, tired of you both, says the school may stay if it does not grow. It grows. Nobody comes back to close it. Years later you hear the teacher has three thousand students across the province, and still teaches the butchers' children first.

fail.log: The magistrate has you both put out of the hall. The school closes. The teacher simply moves it, into a barn, then a ferry shed, then under a bridge, and the children follow. You carry benches every time. (-6 health)

choices.text: Tell them to bend a little, for now

effects.log: "Bend a little," you say. The teacher looks at you with the beast's patience and says, "It did not bend a blade of grass for me. I will not bend this." You have no answer to that. The school stays open, somehow, and you are glad to have been wrong.

events.text: You kept the stone. You do not know why. It sat on your windowsill after the beast went, the one that stopped in the air and fell, and it has never been warm since, not in the hottest summer. Today a peddler of charms offers you real money for it: he has heard the story, and says a stone that a holy beast refused is good luck for gamblers.

choices.text: Sell it to him

effects.log: Eight taels. The peddler goes off delighted. That autumn you trip over nothing three times in a week, and the third time you lie in the lane looking up at the sky thinking that perhaps luck is not the word for what that stone was.

choices.text: Keep it, and carry it with you

effects.log: You tell the peddler it is not for sale. You start carrying it in your sleeve. Every time you are about to hit someone, a neighbour, a mule, a child who has broken a jar, your hand finds the cold stone first, and holds it, and the moment passes.

choices.text: Take it back to the gate and set it down where it fell

effects.log: You put it back in the dust by the gate, exactly where it dropped. By the next morning the weeds round it have grown up in a neat ring, and nobody, for some reason, ever steps on that spot again.

events.text: A hunting party has come through the valley with silk snares and a wagon, asking about a five-coloured deer, and paying well for anyone who has seen one. They have heard that you have. Their leader is pleasant and patient, and the snares in the wagon are very fine, the kind that do not break the skin.

choices.text: Send them the wrong way

effects.log: You send them north, over the pass, toward a valley you know has nothing in it but goats. They go. You walk up to the gate where the beast once stood and stand there a long while, in case it is listening.

choices.text: Show them where it stood, for the money

effects.log: Fifteen taels. They set their snares round the gate, and wait a month, and catch nothing, and go. But you dream for years of a soft hoof caught in silk, and a grandmother with a sickle, and you never find out whether the dream was true.

choices.text: Join them, to make sure they fail

ok.log: You join them, and every snare you set, you set badly, and every track you read, you misread. After a month their leader pays you off with a look that says he knows exactly what you have done. He does not seem entirely sorry.

fail.log: They catch you loosening a snare and give you a beating and send you home. But a snare loosened is a snare loosened. (-8 health)

events.text: Since the night you knelt by the gate with the beast, you cannot walk anywhere without looking down. Today a neighbour's boy is pouring boiling water down an ant hole for fun, and the neighbours are laughing.

choices.text: Stop him, and show him how to wait for them

effects.log: You take the kettle off him. He sulks. You kneel and show him the road, the ants carrying a dead moth between six of them like pallbearers, and he forgets to sulk and kneels too. His mother calls him in at dark and he does not come for a long while.

choices.text: Say nothing, but look down from now on

effects.log: You say nothing. But for the rest of your life you step over ants, and people notice, and some of them start doing it too without knowing why.

events.text: A drought year, and a quarrel in the village over who drew more than their share from the last well. Two families are at the well with buckets and fists. You are standing between them. You notice, in the middle of it, that an ant road crosses the well's stone lip, and that nobody has stepped on it yet.

choices.text: Point at the ants and tell them the story of the beast at the gate

ok.log: You tell it: the beast, the ants, the two nights. It is a strange thing to tell in the middle of a fight, and that is why it works; by the time you finish both families are looking at the ants instead of each other, and someone laughs, and the buckets are shared out by turns.

fail.log: Somebody shoves you halfway through, and you go down on the ant road. You get up and keep telling it, with dust in your hair, and in the end they share the water because you are too ridiculous to fight around. (-5 health)

choices.text: Draw water for both families yourself, turn and turn about

effects.log: You take both buckets and draw, one for each, all afternoon, until your arms shake. Nobody can fight while you are doing that. By evening the well is low but the village is whole.

events.text: You still go to the threshing yard at dawn sometimes, in case. This morning there is a ring of small, careful hoofprints round the weed in the yard stone again, fresh, and a heap of chestnut husks, and nothing else.

choices.text: Leave a heap of fallen chestnuts in the yard

effects.log: You gather fallen ones only, the way it did, and leave them in a heap. In the morning the heap is gone and the husks are piled neatly by the wall. You do it every autumn for the rest of your childhood, and every autumn the husks are piled.

choices.text: Hide behind the straw stack and wait for it

ok.log: You wait until your legs go to sleep, and then it comes: bigger now, the bud on its brow a short horn with a soft tip. It knows you are there. It eats its chestnuts and looks straight at the straw stack once, politely, and goes.

fail.log: You fall asleep behind the straw stack and wake with a cold. The hoofprints are there, round the weed, and round the straw stack too, very close. (-2 health)

events.text: Grown now, you are at the royal post-station stables, or a lord's, or a sect's, and the head groom shows off a strange new bridle: silk, soft as moss, made to catch "the five-coloured colt" that the grooms have been seeing in the far pasture at dawn. He wants a volunteer who is good with skittish beasts.

choices.text: Volunteer, and lose the bridle in the river

effects.log: You take the bridle out to the far pasture, sit on the riverbank at dawn, and drop it in. It floats away like a strand of weed. When you look up the colt, not a colt any more, is standing on the far bank, and dips its horned head to you once before it goes into the mist.

choices.text: Tell the groom what you saw as a child

ok.log: You tell it, the weed and the chestnuts and the bridle you put on and took off again. The groom listens to the end, a rough old man, and then hangs the silk bridle on a nail in the tack room and never takes it down.

fail.log: The groom laughs at you for a child's dream, and sends someone else. They come back with nothing, a week later, and a fever. The silk bridle hangs on a nail after that, and nobody mentions it.

events.text: {npc}, the bounty hunter from the ford, finds you at an inn on the river road a year after the three days. {npc} has given up bounty work. "I keep dreaming of it standing on the water," {npc} says. "I want to know what it is. Somebody at the temple upriver says there are old books."

choices.text: Go upriver with {npc} to the old books

effects.log: Three days upriver, a temple with a library of mouldy scrolls and one monk who can read them. The monk finds the passage: a beast that does not tread on living insects nor break living grass, whose horn ends in flesh, that has martial power and does not use it. {npc} reads it twice and then goes out and sits by the river for a long time, and you leave {npc} there.

choices.text: Tell {npc} some things are better not named

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time and then laughs, the first laugh you have heard from {npc}. "You sound like it," {npc} says. You drink to the beast that would not fight, and {npc} goes upriver alone in the morning.

events.text: Years after the ford. A young swordsman comes to your gate with a challenge, as young swordsmen do, having heard of you. You look at the eager face, the cheap sword, the bad stance, and remember three days on a riverbank fighting something that would not fight back.

choices.text: Fight the way it fought you: never strike

ok.log: You never strike. You are behind the youngster, then beside, then simply not there, from noon until the cheap sword droops. The youngster sits down in the dust, bewildered, and asks what that was. You find you are smiling. "Something I was taught," you say, "by somebody who never once hit me."

fail.log: You try never to strike and the youngster, much quicker than the stance suggested, lands three cuts on you before you get the rhythm. But you get it. In the end the youngster is the one who sits down. (-8 health)

choices.text: Beat the youngster quickly and send them home

effects.log: Three moves and the cheap sword is in the dust. The youngster goes home with a sore wrist and a lesson. It is a good lesson. It is not the one you were given at the ford, and you know it.

events.text: {npc}, the old scholar who wept into a sleeve at the lord's western hunt, sends for you. The letter is in a hand that shakes. {npc} is dying, and says there is something to tell you about the beast in the cart, and about a ribbon a mother tied all those years ago.

choices.text: Go at once

effects.log: {npc} tells it in a whisper, propped on pillows: a poor house, a long labour, a beast at the gate, a mother who tied a ribbon to its horn and swore the child would be something. "I was the child," {npc} says. "It came for my birth. And it came again at the end, and they had broken its leg." {npc} dies two days later with a hand in yours. You hear afterward that the night before, something stood at the gate till dawn.

choices.text: Send a physician, and come when you can

effects.log: You send the best physician you know. By the time you come yourself, {npc} is in the ground. The physician tells you there was a beast at the gate the last night, and that the old scholar went out to it in a night robe, against all advice, and came back smiling, and slept.

events.text: The lord of the western hunt is dead, and his heir has invited you to the autumn hunt in the west, as a power heaven listens to. The heir is young and has heard the story of the beast in the cart from three sides. "Tell me what really happened," the heir says, "and tell me what I should do if they bring one in."

choices.text: Tell the heir to let it go the moment it is seen

effects.log: "Let it go," you say. "And then look at your provinces very hard, because it only comes when something is about to be born or about to die." The heir writes that down. The western hunt is held every year after that, and the hunters are told what not to bring in.

choices.text: Tell the heir to stop holding the hunt

ok.log: The heir looks shocked, then thoughtful, then relieved, as if you had said aloud a thing the heir had been afraid to think. The western hunt is not held again. The forests in the west fill up with roe deer so tame that children feed them.

fail.log: The heir laughs and holds the hunt anyway. But the beaters, you hear, have been quietly told by someone that a scaled thing with a soft horn is to be driven away, not in. You suspect the heir.

events.text: Your cousin, heavy with child, has had the conception dream everyone hopes for, and tells it to the whole lane: a beast like a deer, covered in scales of five colours and giving off light, walked in through the gate and lay down on the porch. The fortune-teller says a gentle child, or a child of great talent, or both. Your cousin's family is already talking about examinations and a post at court. The child is not born yet.

choices.text: Say a gentle child is a good enough thing to be

effects.log: "Gentle is enough," you say. Your cousin's family looks at you as if you had spat on the porch. Your cousin, though, lays a hand on the belly and says quietly, "Yes. That is what it felt like. Gentle."

choices.text: Ask exactly what the beast did in the dream

effects.log: Your cousin thinks. "It stepped round the hen," your cousin says slowly. "The hen was asleep in the gateway and it stepped round. It took a long time." Nobody else thinks this is the important part. You do.

choices.text: Join in the talk of examinations

effects.log: You join in. By evening the unborn child has passed the examinations, become a minister, and saved the kingdom twice. Your cousin, in the middle of it all, looks tired.

events.text: The dream-child is a small child now, and gentle, and slow at letters, and cries when the boys of the lane drown kittens. Your cousin's family has decided the dream was wrong, and is not quiet about it, and the child has heard.

choices.text: Take the child out to look at things that are small

effects.log: You take the child to the stream, the beetles, the frog spawn, the ant road under the eaves. The child knows the names of none of them and the habits of all of them already. "Is that a talent?" the child asks. "It is the talent," you say, and you believe it.

choices.text: Speak to the family for the child

ok.log: "The dream said gentle first," you remind them, "and you only heard the second word." They are ashamed, a little, and stop saying it in front of the child, which is something.

fail.log: They tell you to mind your own house. The child, who was listening behind the door, comes and stands next to you anyway.

events.text: Many years on, the dream-child is the village's healer of animals: oxen with colic, dogs with thorns, a hawk once, carried in from the hills in a basket. Never a minister. The family has stopped mentioning the dream. And last night, the healer tells you, the dream came back: the five-coloured beast, standing at the gate, waiting for a hen.

choices.text: Tell the healer it came to see how things turned out

effects.log: "It came to see," you say. The healer laughs, and then does not laugh, and goes out to the gate and stands there for a while in the dawn looking at the dust, where there is a very careful line of small hoofprints going round the place where the hen sleeps.

choices.text: Ask the healer to set your old ox's leg

effects.log: The healer sets your old ox's leg with hands so gentle the ox does not even shift its cud. You think: that is the talent the dream meant. You are certain of it, and the ox walks for six more years.

events.text: The village has started calling you a gireuna, a qilin-child, the kind that grows up great. You recited the whole Thousand Character Classic at the new year and the teacher wept. Now the older children wait for you behind the woodpile after lessons, and the elders talk about you in front of you as if you were a promising calf.

choices.text: Hide how much you know

effects.log: You start getting things wrong on purpose. The older children leave you alone. The teacher looks at you sadly and says nothing. You keep a second set of lessons in your head, the real ones, and recite them to the hens.

choices.text: Keep reciting, and take the beatings

effects.log: You keep reciting. You get thumped behind the woodpile every third day. It does not stop you. It also, you notice, makes you very careful never to thump anyone yourself. (-4 health)

choices.text: Ask what a qilin actually is

effects.log: The teacher is delighted to be asked. A beast that will not step on a living insect, nor break a living blade of grass, whose horn ends in soft flesh so that it cannot wound. "So a qilin-child," you say slowly, "is a child who does not hit back." The teacher opens their mouth, and shuts it, and says that is not what the village means, but perhaps it should be.

events.text: Grown, you are no great anything. A clerk, a farmer, a hired sword, an ordinary person, and the old people of the village, who called you a gireuna, look at you with a disappointment they think is kind. Then a child of the lane, very bright, starts being called gireuna too, and you see the older children waiting behind the woodpile.

choices.text: Walk the child home every day after lessons

effects.log: Every day, for three years. Nobody touches the child. The child grows up to be no great anything either, and very happy, and says much later that you were the only person who never once asked them to be great.

choices.text: Tell the elders to stop calling the child that

ok.log: "It is a heavy word," you tell them, "and you are not the ones who carry it." To your surprise, they listen. The child is just a child after that, and runs about the lane with the others.

fail.log: They tell you that you are bitter because the word did not come true for you. Perhaps. You walk the child home anyway.

events.text: A rich hunter from the capital has hired you to carry his nets: fine silk snares, soft as hair, that will hold a foreleg without breaking the skin. He is after a five-coloured deer that has been seen in the high pines, and he wants it alive, for a lord who collects omens. On the second morning you find its tracks: slender, cloven, and going all the long way round every fern shoot on the path.

choices.text: Show the hunter the tracks

effects.log: Six taels extra for sharp eyes. The hunter strings his snares along the trail all day, whistling. That night you lie awake listening to the forest, and hear, very far off, something like a temple bell, though there is no temple.

choices.text: Scuff the tracks out before the hunter sees them

effects.log: You scuff them out with your sandal, carefully, without treading on the ferns. It takes a long time. When you straighten up, there is a fresh set of tracks a little way off, going round the place you just scuffed, as if something had stood there watching you do it.

choices.text: Follow the tracks alone, to see it first

ok.log: You follow them to a clearing, and it is there, drinking dew off the low leaves. It lifts its head and looks at you. It does not run. After a while you understand that it is waiting for you to decide what kind of person you are, and that it will wait as long as that takes.

fail.log: You lose the tracks and your footing at once and slide down a gully on your back. At the bottom, sitting in the stream, you see the tracks again, on the far bank, going away. (-6 health)

events.text: The silk snare has caught it. You hear it before you see it: not a scream, only a long breath. It is standing very still with one foreleg held fast in the silk, and the hunter is coming up through the pines with a cart. It could kick the snare post out of the ground, you think, or kick you. It does neither. It is looking at a beetle on the snare post, which it would crush if it pulled.

choices.text: Cut the snare before the hunter comes

effects.log: You cut it with your knife. The beast does not bolt. It waits until the beetle has walked off the post, and then goes, unhurried, into the pines. The hunter arrives to an empty snare and a hired porter with a knife, and you walk home without wages, and do not mind.

choices.text: Move the beetle off the post

effects.log: You pick up the beetle and set it on a fern. The beast pulls, once, and the post comes out of the ground and the silk falls away, and it is gone into the trees before the hunter reaches the clearing. It could have done that the whole time. It was waiting for the beetle.

choices.text: Help the hunter load it into the cart

effects.log: Twelve taels. It does not struggle at all, which is worse than if it had. Three days later the hunter comes back to the village alone and very quiet, and says the cart was empty in the morning, and the ropes still tied.

events.text: The rope bridge over the river breaks in the summer flood while you are on it. The water takes you under, and turns you over, and you are going to drown, and then something lifts you. Something under you, warm, and smooth, and walking. On the water. You come to on the far bank, coughing, alone. There is nothing on the river but brown water, and on the bank beside you, a ring of hoofprints in the mud that you did not make.

choices.text: Leave an offering on the bank

effects.log: You have nothing but your last rice cake. You put it on a flat stone by the hoofprints. In the morning the rice cake is still there, untouched, and a sparrow is eating it. You think that is probably the answer.

choices.text: Search the river for whatever it was

effects.log: You walk the bank for two days, calling. You find nothing but a ferry child on the far side who says the old people say a beast lives in the rapids upriver, that walks on the water and never steps on a fish. (-4 health)

choices.text: Tell nobody: they would not believe you

effects.log: You tell nobody. But every time you cross a river after that, you look down at the water as if it might be looking up.

events.text: Another flood year, and this time you are on the bank, and a ferry child is in the water, and the river is the same brown animal it was the day it took you.

choices.text: Go in after the child

ok.log: You go in, and get the child, and the river tries to take you both, and then the water under your feet goes firm, for three strides, as if you were walking on the back of something. You reach the bank. You do not look back. You know what you would see.

fail.log: You go in and the river beats you against the rocks, but you hold the child up, and something lifts the two of you at the last moment and sets you on the stones. You are badly hurt. The child is not hurt at all. (-12 health)

choices.text: Throw a rope and shout for help

effects.log: You throw a rope and miss, and throw again, and the child gets it, and the village pulls. When the child is out you notice that the rope never once went taut, as if the child had been standing on something.

events.text: You are older now, and you still cross rivers looking down. Today, at the ford below the rapids, a monk you have never met stops you and asks, out of nowhere, whether you are the one who was carried. The monk says the beast of the rapids keeps a count of everyone it has carried across, and that you are on it.

choices.text: Ask how many are on the count

effects.log: "Not many," the monk says. "It does not like to be seen doing it. Eleven in all its long years. You are the ninth." You walk home slowly, feeling like a word in a very short, very old poem.

choices.text: Ask the monk to tell it thank you

effects.log: "It knows," the monk says. "It knew when you put the rice cake on the stone." You never told anyone about the rice cake. Perhaps you did not need to.

events.text: You have fallen in with a band of hill bandits, for reasons that seemed good at the time. In a storm the chief leads you all into a dry cave above the rapids. There is straw in it, very old, and a smell like warm hay and incense. In the night you go out to relieve yourself and find a beast standing in the rain outside its own cave, getting soaked, and looking at the loose boulder above the entrance as if it had been thinking about it, and had decided not to.

choices.text: Wake the chief and tell the band to leave

ok.log: You wake the chief and say only that this is somebody's home. The chief, half-asleep, sees something over your shoulder in the rain and goes very pale, and gets everyone up and out without a word. The beast walks back into the dry as you pass, and lies down in the old straw, and sighs.

fail.log: The chief cuffs you and goes back to sleep. You sit outside in the rain with the beast until dawn instead, both of you dripping, neither of you saying anything. (-5 health)

choices.text: Stand in the rain with it until morning

effects.log: You stand in the rain beside it until dawn. When the bandits wake and file out, you are not one of them any more: you have decided. You leave the band that morning and walk down the mountain, wet through and lighter. (-3 health)

events.text: Years after the storm at the cave, the old bandit chief is in the stocks in a market town, and recognises you in the crowd. "You saw it too," the chief croaks. "That night. I have been trying to be a better thief ever since. It did not work."

choices.text: Pay the fine and take the chief home with you (15 taels)

effects.log: Fifteen taels. The old chief comes home with you and splits your firewood for the rest of a long life, very badly, and never steals so much as a persimmon. Once, merry at the new year, the chief says it was not the beast's look that did it. It was that the beast got wet so as not to wake them.

choices.text: Give the chief water, and walk on

effects.log: You hold up a dipper of water. The chief drinks and says thank you, and you walk on. Some kindnesses are only a dipper wide. That is still a kindness.

events.text: There is a meadow above your village that nobody mows. Nobody can tell you why; it is simply not done. This summer the harvest is thin and the oxen are hungry, and the headman has said that this year, old custom or not, the meadow comes down. You have been given a scythe.

choices.text: Mow it, as the headman says

effects.log: You mow it in two days. The hay is sweet and the oxen are glad of it. On the third morning there is a line of slender hoofprints across the stubble, going up into the hills, and none coming back.

choices.text: Walk the meadow first and look

effects.log: You walk it end to end. In the middle there is a line of slender hoofprints crossing it, fresh, and every blade of grass on that line is standing straight. You put the scythe down. When you tell the headman, the headman goes up and looks, and comes back, and the oxen are fed from somewhere else.

choices.text: Ask the oldest person in the village

effects.log: The oldest person in the village is a toothless great-grandmother who laughs at you for a long time. "Something walks there," she says at last, "that does not like grass broken. If you mow it, it walks somewhere else. Then what will we have?" You do not know what she means. You leave the meadow standing.

events.text: A war band of some lord's soldiers comes over the hill and pitches camp right at the edge of the unmown meadow. The captain wants it cut for horse fodder, and the village to do the cutting.

choices.text: Tell the captain the meadow is holy

ok.log: You tell it as if you believed it, and halfway through you find you do. The captain, a superstitious soldier, looks at the grass for a long time and moves the camp. The next day the war goes somewhere else. Nobody can prove the two things are connected.

fail.log: The captain laughs and has you pushed into the ditch. But in the night the horses will not graze the meadow, not one of them, and in the morning the war band moves on, cursing. (-6 health)

choices.text: Cut it yourself, slowly, a strip at a time

effects.log: You cut so slowly that the war band moves on before you have finished the first strip. You never finish it. The cut strip grows back by autumn, greener than the rest.

events.text: You burn charcoal on the ridge, and this dry autumn your kiln has set the pines alight. The fire runs uphill faster than a horse. You are running down. And going up, into the fire, against everything that lives, is a slender beast with pale flames round its hooves, and as you watch it comes back down out of the smoke with a fawn in its mouth, and sets it down, and goes back up.

choices.text: Go back up with it

ok.log: You go up with it. A badger in a burrow, a nest of hares, an old dog someone left chained. Every time you come down with something, the beast is coming down too, its flames curling round your ankles and not burning you. By dawn the ridge is black and the hollow at the bottom is full of animals sitting very still, side by side, and not one of them eats another.

fail.deathCause: went back into the fire on the ridge
fail.log: The fire takes you on the second climb. You fall in the smoke, and something lifts you by the collar the way it lifted the fawn, and carries you down, and sets you on the stones. You live, burned. (-25 health)

choices.text: Dig a firebreak across the bottom of the slope

effects.log: You dig until your hands bleed. The fire comes down to your trench and stops. Behind it the beast is bringing down the last of the animals, and when you look up from the trench it is standing on the far side of the flames, looking at your ditch as if it approved of ditches.

choices.text: Run, and save yourself

effects.log: You run. You live. In the morning, from the village, you see the ridge black from end to end, and in the hollow at its foot a crowd of animals, fawns and hares and badgers, sitting quietly together in the ash. You know it was your kiln. You do not burn charcoal again.

events.text: The ridge you burned has grown back: young pines, a thicket of bush clover, deer. You have been planting it, a seedling at a time, for years. This spring, at dawn, you see the beast up there among your young trees, grazing on the dew, careful of every seedling.

choices.text: Plant one more, right where it stands

effects.log: You climb up with a seedling. It steps aside, exactly far enough, and watches you plant it. When you stand up with dirt on your knees it is gone, and the seedling has dew on it already.

choices.text: Leave it in peace

effects.log: You stay below and watch until the sun is up. It is the first time since the fire that you have looked at the ridge without shame.

events.text: You help keep the village school, such as it is: twelve children, a leaking roof, one copy of each primer. One of the twelve is a child from a hovel by the river who reads before anyone has taught them, and asks questions you cannot answer, and gets the others asking too. The headman's family pays the most and wants the child gone.

choices.text: Throw the child out, as the headman wants

effects.log: You throw the child out. Five taels from the headman for the roof. That night you dream of a beast standing in the rain outside a schoolroom door, getting wet, waiting for someone to open it. You wake ashamed.

choices.text: Keep the child, and lose the headman's money

effects.log: You keep the child. The headman's children leave, and their money, and the roof leaks worse. The child brings a ladder and some reeds and fixes it, badly, and then asks why rain falls down and not up.

choices.text: Teach the child at night, alone

effects.log: By day the child is gone; by night, by a rush lamp, you teach the child everything you know. It takes four winters. In the fifth the child starts teaching you.

events.text: Word comes from the far side of the province: a teacher with no post and no hall, teaching anyone who will sit down, has three thousand students. People say a five-coloured beast stood at that teacher's gate the night they were born. It is the child from your school.

choices.text: Walk across the province to sit in the back of a lesson

effects.log: You sit at the back among farmers and butchers' children. The teacher sees you, and stops in the middle of a sentence, and bows to you in front of three thousand people. You go red to the ears. Afterward the teacher says only, "You were first."

choices.text: Stay home and mend the school roof

effects.log: You stay home and mend the roof properly at last. There are more children in the school now than there ever were, because people have heard where the teacher started.

events.text: Word comes from the far side of the province: the child you threw out of your school has grown into a teacher with no post and no hall, and three thousand students. You never forgot the face.

choices.text: Go and ask forgiveness

effects.log: The teacher listens, and laughs, and says: "You taught me the first thing. That a door can close. I have spent my life opening them." You do not know whether that is forgiveness. It is something better.

choices.text: Keep away, and open your own door wider

effects.log: You go home and take anyone who comes, from that day: the river children, the butchers', the slaves'. The roof leaks. You do not mind.

events.text: Your sect's elder has sent you to the market town on an errand: buy one packet of qilin horn shavings, for an elixir of long life. The apothecary has them, at a price that would feed a family for a year. Through the curtain behind the counter you can see the apothecary's boy scraping a cow horn into paper packets.

choices.text: Buy them anyway: it is the elder's money and the elder's errand

effects.log: You buy them and bring them back. The elder brews the elixir and drinks it and declares that it is working. You keep your mouth shut. It is, after all, very good cow.

choices.text: Call the apothecary a cheat, loudly

ok.log: You pull the curtain back in front of the whole market. The apothecary's boy freezes with the cow horn in one hand. The crowd laughs until it cries. You go home without shavings and with the purse full, and the elder, after a long silence, laughs too.

fail.log: The apothecary's cousins are large, and the market is the apothecary's market. You leave in a hurry with a split lip and no shavings. (-6 health)

choices.text: Ask the apothecary whether anyone has ever seen a real one

effects.log: The apothecary looks at you for a long time and then, surprisingly, tells the truth. "Nobody has ever sold a real one," the apothecary says. "Its horn ends in flesh. There is nothing to scrape. The only way to get a shaving would be to make it bleed, and nobody who has ever seen it could do that."

events.text: On the road home from the market you stop to water your horse at a ford, and on the far bank a slender beast in small scales is drinking. It lifts its head and looks at the packet sticking out of your sleeve, and you could swear it looks amused.

choices.text: Throw the packet in the river

effects.log: The packet floats off, cow horn and all. The beast watches it go and then looks back at you and blows through its nose, like a horse laughing. When you have finished watering your horse it is gone, and the far bank is unmarked, not a reed bent.

choices.text: Cross the ford to it

ok.log: It lets you come close enough to see the horn. The tip is soft and rounded and warm-coloured, like the pad of a thumb. There is nothing on it to scrape. It touches the tip, lightly, to your empty sleeve, and walks away across the water.

fail.log: You slip on the stones and go in up to your neck. When you come up it is on the bank you just left, beside your horse, which is not afraid of it at all. (-4 health)

events.text: There is a story going round the inns: a beast in the mountains that has never lost a fight and has never wounded anyone. Masters go up to fight it and come down unhurt, and do not talk about it. You are at the height of your skill, and tired of stories. You go up.

choices.text: Fight it as hard as you can

ok.log: You use everything. It is never where you strike. At dusk you are on your knees in the leaves with your sword arm dead, and it has not touched you once, and you are not hurt anywhere but your pride. It stands over you and lowers its horn, and the soft tip touches your forehead like a thumb, and you understand you have lost, and that it is the best fight of your life.

fail.log: You use everything and it is never there, and halfway through the afternoon you fall over your own feet trying to turn too fast and crack your head on a stone. When you wake it is lying beside you, keeping the flies off your face with its tail. (-8 health)

choices.text: Watch it for a day before you fight

effects.log: You watch it all day. It grazes on dew. It steps round snails. A hawk drops on a hare and it puts itself between them without hurry, and the hawk sheers off. At dusk you put your sword in its sheath and go down the mountain, and you do not talk about it either.

events.text: A second time up the mountain. This time you have brought no sword. You have come to ask it to teach you what it did, and you are not sure how one asks a beast for that.

choices.text: Kneel, as a disciple kneels to a master

effects.log: You kneel. It walks round you once, slowly. Then it goes and stands in the stream, and waits, and after a long while you understand that you are meant to stand in the stream too, and not move, and not disturb the little fish. You stand there until dark. You come back the next day, and the next, for a year.

choices.text: Copy the way it walks

effects.log: You follow it about, putting your feet where it puts its feet, which is never on anything alive. By the end of the summer you can cross a meadow without leaving a trace. Your footwork is the best in the province. You never explain where it came from.

events.text: A duel to the death, sworn in the old way, against a sect enemy who has wronged your house. The courtyard is full. You have the better art. You also have, now, a year of standing in a stream not disturbing fish.

choices.text: Win without wounding

ok.log: You are never where the blade is. An hour in, your enemy is exhausted and unmarked, and you are standing behind them with an empty hand on their shoulder. "To the death," someone in the crowd says, uncertainly. You walk out of the ring. Your enemy sits down in the dust and weeps, and years later sends their children to learn from you.

fail.log: You will not strike, and it costs you: a cut along the arm, another on the ribs. But you are never where the killing blow is, and in the end your enemy throws the sword down in disgust and fury and walks out of the ring. You are alive. So are they. (-12 health)

choices.text: End it the way duels end

effects.log: You end it. The crowd cheers. That night you go up the mountain and the beast is not there, and it is not there the next night, or ever again.

events.text: The orthodox and unorthodox factions are holding peace talks in a lake pavilion, and you are one of the guards on the railing. The witness the two sides could agree on is not a person. It is standing at the head of the table: a slender beast in five-coloured scales, with a soft-tipped horn, very still. {npc}, a steward of the unorthodox side, is pouring the tea. You see {npc}'s thumbnail tap the rim of one cup, and a little grey powder fall in.

choices.text: Knock the cup out of the hand that reaches for it

effects.log: You are across the pavilion before you have decided to move, and the cup goes spinning into the lake. Swords come out on both sides. The beast takes one step forward, and every sword stops, and a voice like a temple bell says, very quietly, "Sit down." They sit. {npc} is led away, untouched, at the beast's look.

choices.text: Seize {npc} before anyone notices

ok.log: You have {npc} by the wrist and out of the pavilion before the cup is lifted. Nobody notices but the beast, which turns its head and watches you go with an expression you will think about for years: not approval. Something sadder, as if it had been hoping {npc} would change their mind on their own.

fail.log: {npc} is quicker than you and there is a knife. You take it in the forearm. The noise stops the talks, and the cup is never drunk. (-10 health)

choices.text: Say nothing and watch what the beast does

effects.log: The cup is set before the orthodox sect's head. The beast steps forward and lowers its head and drinks from it, the whole cup, slowly. Then it stands there for the rest of the talks, swaying a little, its eyes on {npc}. Nobody understands what has happened but you. And {npc}, who goes white, and kneels, and confesses before the evening is out.

events.text: {npc}, the steward who poisoned the tea at the peace talks, was not executed: the beast would not allow it, and both sides had sworn to abide by its word. Years later {npc} finds you. "It made me a gardener at the lake pavilion," {npc} says. "All these years. I want to know why it did not let them kill me."

choices.text: Tell {npc}: because then the talks would have been about you

effects.log: {npc} thinks about that for a long time. "So I was not worth killing," {npc} says at last. "No," you say. "The peace was worth more than your death." {npc} goes back to the lake pavilion and gardens there until the end, and the peace holds, mostly.

choices.text: Tell {npc} you do not know, and that you have wondered too

effects.log: You sit together on the pavilion steps and wonder, out loud, for an afternoon. Neither of you works it out. It is a good afternoon anyway.

events.text: Your sect leader has decided that the coming war against the rival sect will be fought "under the qilin". A great banner is being painted with the five-coloured beast on it, and the leader wants you to take a painter into the mountains to sketch the real one, so the banner is true.
events.arc: Under the Sign of the Beast

choices.text: Go, and bring back a false sketch

effects.log: You take the painter up the mountain and down the wrong valleys for a month and bring back a sketch of a mountain goat with a candle on its head. The banner goes up anyway, goat and all, and the disciples laugh at it, and morale is poor, and the war, oddly, does not quite start.

choices.text: Go, and find it, and let it decide

ok.log: You find it at a spring. The painter sets up the brushes and the beast simply walks away, every time, until the painter gives up and paints it walking away. The banner shows a beast with its back to the viewer, going into the trees. The sect leader is furious. The disciples, looking at it, go very quiet.

fail.log: You find nothing but rain and a sprained ankle. The painter invents the beast from old books. It has two horns, wings, and a lion's face. It is not the beast at all, and you are glad. (-5 health)

choices.text: Refuse the errand

effects.log: "It does not fight," you tell the sect leader. "Fighting under it is a lie." The sect leader has you kneel in the hall for a day and a night. You kneel. You do not change your mind.

events.text: The war came anyway. The banner with the beast is carried at the front of your sect's charge, and on the far hill the rival sect has painted the same beast on theirs. Two armies of martial artists are about to kill each other under two pictures of a creature that has never harmed anything.
events.arc: Under the Sign of the Beast

choices.text: Lower your sect's banner

ok.log: You take the pole from the bearer and lower it to the ground. Across the field, after a long moment, the other banner comes down too. Nobody charges. The two sect leaders meet in the middle of the field to shout at each other, and shouting is better than the other thing.

fail.log: Your own side knocks you down for it and raises the banner again. But it was down long enough that the charge lost its moment, and the fight, when it comes, is short and half-hearted, and few die. (-10 health)

choices.text: Fight, and keep your own hands clean of killing

effects.log: You fight with the flat of the blade all day. It is harder than killing. In the evening you look up at the banner, torn and muddy, and the painted beast looks back at you from it with a patience you do not deserve. (-8 health)

events.text: An alchemist with a famous name wants to hire you. The alchemist does not want the five-coloured beast killed, or even caught: "Only the tip," the alchemist says, holding up a little silver knife. "The soft tip of the horn. It grows back. A thumbnail's worth, for the elixir of the hundred years. It will hardly feel it."

choices.text: Ask whether anyone has asked the beast

effects.log: The alchemist blinks. Nobody has ever asked that. "It is a beast," the alchemist says. "So were we," you say, "until somebody asked." The alchemist puts the silver knife down and does not pick it up again while you are in the room.

choices.text: Take the job, and warn the beast

ok.log: You take the money and go into the hills ahead of the alchemist's people, and find it at a spring, and tell it plainly what is coming. It listens with its ears turned to you. When the alchemist's people reach the spring there is nothing there but a heap of fallen chestnuts, neatly piled.

fail.log: You take the money and go to warn it and get lost, and the alchemist's people find you before they find it, and work out what you are doing. They take half the money back with their fists. They never find the beast. (-6 health)

choices.text: Refuse outright

effects.log: You refuse. The alchemist shrugs and hires someone else. You hear later the someone else came back from the hills with no tip and no knife and no wish to talk about it, and went to work in a rice paddy.

events.text: The alchemist who wanted the tip of the horn is dying, at the end of a long and famous life, and has sent for you. On the table beside the bed is the little silver knife, never used, polished to a mirror.

choices.text: Ask why the knife was never used

effects.log: "I found it," the alchemist says. "Years after you. I stood in front of it with the knife. It lowered its head for me, for the cut, as if I had asked politely. I could not. Nobody could." The alchemist puts the knife in your hand. "Throw it in a river. A deep one." You do.

choices.text: Sit with the alchemist until the end

effects.log: You sit. Near dawn the alchemist sighs and says, "The elixir of the hundred years was always the wrong question," and dies smiling. In the courtyard, when you go out, every blade of grass is silvered with dew and none of it is bent.

events.text: {npc}, an orphan of your house whom you are raising, is eight, and the sect elders have started calling {npc} qilin-like: the quickest mind any of them has seen. They mean it as praise, at first. Now they mean it as a plan: they want {npc} in the inner court at once, on the fighting path, to become the sect's sword. {npc} cries when made to hit the practice post.

choices.text: Keep {npc} out of the inner court

ok.log: You argue with the elders until they are sick of the sight of you. {npc} stays in the outer court, reading, drawing beasts in the dust, learning medicine from the old cook. The elders call it a waste. {npc} calls you, once, by accident, the wrong word for a guardian, the one that means more, and goes red.

fail.log: The elders overrule you. {npc} goes to the inner court. You go every evening to the edge of the training yard and sit there, so that {npc} can see you, and that is all you can do.

choices.text: Let the elders have {npc}: it is a great honour

effects.log: {npc} goes to the inner court. {npc} is very good. In two years {npc} is the best sword of that age in the sect, and has stopped drawing anything in the dust at all.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what {npc} wants

effects.log: Nobody has asked before. {npc} thinks about it for a whole day, and then says: "I want to make the hurt things better." You go to the elders with that, and it is a harder argument, and a better one.

events.text: {npc} is grown, a healer of the sect's wounded, and the elders have decided again: the war needs swords, not bandages, and {npc} with the quickest mind in the sect is to lead the vanguard. {npc} comes to you the night before, white-faced. "They say a qilin-like child should be the one in front," {npc} says. "I thought a qilin was the one that does not fight."

choices.text: Tell {npc} to refuse, and stand beside {npc} when {npc} does

effects.log: {npc} refuses, in the main hall, before every elder. You stand beside {npc}. You are both put out of the inner court. {npc} sets up a healer's hut at the foot of the mountain, and the wounded of both sides come to it, and in a few years it is the most respected place in the province.

choices.text: Go in front yourself, in {npc}'s place

ok.log: You lead the vanguard yourself. You come back. {npc} is waiting at the hut with bandages, and uses them on you, and does not say anything, and does not need to.

fail.log: You lead the vanguard yourself and come back on a door. {npc} saves your life over three days and nights. You are not good for the vanguard again. {npc} does not seem sorry about that. (-20 health)

events.text: {npc}, the ward you let the elders have, is the sect's sword now, famous and feared, and has come home for a visit. At dinner {npc} says, offhand, that on the road a strange beast in five-coloured scales stood in the path and would not move, and that {npc} nearly cut it down, and then could not, and does not know why.

choices.text: Tell {npc} about the dust drawings

effects.log: "You used to draw it," you say. "In the dust, every day, before they took you." {npc} puts down the cup very slowly. The next morning {npc} goes to the edge of the training yard and kneels, and draws in the dust with a stick, badly, for a long time.

choices.text: Say nothing, and wonder

effects.log: You say nothing. {npc} goes back to the war. But you hear, the next year, that the famous sword of your sect has started letting beaten enemies walk away, and nobody knows why.

events.text: A plague has come to the river villages, and you have come with your art to keep the bandits off the medicine carts. The healer in charge is {npc}, young, plain-robed, who walks into every house the others will not. People say a five-coloured beast stood at {npc}'s gate the night {npc} was born and a red ribbon was tied to its horn. {npc} asks you to put your sword down and carry water.

choices.text: Carry water

effects.log: You carry water for forty days. You watch {npc} sit with the dying and hold their hands and never once look afraid. On the thirty-ninth night you see a slender beast standing at the end of the lane in the dark, watching {npc} work, and it does not come closer, and it does not leave.

choices.text: Keep guarding the carts: that is what you are for

effects.log: You guard the carts. Twice bandits come, and twice you send them off. The medicine gets through. {npc} thanks you, properly, and you understand that both things were needed, and that only one of them was brave.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you what your hands can do here

ok.log: {npc} teaches you to press the points that ease a fever, to make the bitter tea, to sit with someone at the end. Your qi turns out to be good for it. By the time the plague passes you are a healer's apprentice as well as a martial artist, and you are not sure which you are prouder of.

fail.log: You try and you take the fever yourself. {npc} nurses you through it, scolding the whole time. (-10 health)

events.text: {npc} has been offered a place in a great poison sect, the only school that truly knows the plague's nature. They will teach {npc} everything. They want, in return, one poison made for them, for a rival. {npc} asks what you think, and looks very tired.

choices.text: Tell {npc}: a healer who makes one poison is a poisoner

effects.log: {npc} closes the eyes, and opens them, and says, "Yes." The poison sect's offer is refused. {npc} learns the plague's nature the slow way, by sitting with it, for ten more years. It works. You hear that on the day the cure was first given, a beast stood at the end of the lane.

choices.text: Offer to stand between {npc} and the sect's anger

ok.log: The poison sect sends people to change {npc}'s mind. They meet you first. They go home. {npc} never makes the poison, and finds the cure anyway.

fail.log: The poison sect sends people. You are not enough for them. But {npc} has had time to leave, and does, and finds the cure in another province. (-16 health)

events.text: {npc} is old, and dying, in a hut full of medicine jars, with students crowded in the yard. {npc} has sent for you because, {npc} says, you were the first one who put down a sword to carry water. Outside the gate, very still, something is waiting.

choices.text: Open the gate for what is waiting

effects.log: You open it. A beast in five-coloured scales walks into the yard, and the students part for it without a sound, and it goes to {npc}'s bedside and lowers its head. {npc} reaches up with a shaking hand and unties a faded red ribbon from its horn. When the ribbon comes away, the red scales along its flank flare like coals, and stay. {npc} dies holding the ribbon, smiling.

choices.text: Hold {npc}'s hand, and let it come in its own time

effects.log: You hold {npc}'s hand. Near dawn you feel a warmth at your back, and do not turn round. {npc} looks past you, and says, "Oh, there you are," in the voice of a child, and is gone. When you turn there is nothing in the doorway, and on the floor a red ribbon, untied.

events.text: You hold a post at court, and the king has given you an order. His reign has been hard: famine, revolt, a purge. The scholars whisper that a true king's reign brings the qilin. So the king will have one. You are to take soldiers and a cage of gilded timber into the mountains, catch the five-coloured beast that the hunters keep seeing, and bring it to the palace as proof.

choices.text: Go, and come back with an empty cage

effects.log: You lead the soldiers round the mountains for a season, very thoroughly, in all the places it is not. You come back with an empty cage and a report so detailed that the king falls asleep halfway through it. You are demoted. You sleep very well.

choices.text: Go, find it, and tell it why you have come

ok.log: You find it alone, on a ridge, and tell it the truth: the king, the cage, the reign. It looks at the cage on its cart far below, and then at you, and walks down the ridge toward it. It walks into the cage itself and lies down. And in the morning the door is open, and the cage is empty, and the lock is unbroken, and the soldiers will not meet your eye.

fail.log: You never find it. You find a great many brambles. You come back with the empty cage and the king's displeasure. (-6 health)

choices.text: Refuse the order to the king's face

ok.log: "Majesty," you say, "if it must be caged to come, it has not come." The court goes silent. The king looks at you for a long time, and then, to everyone's astonishment, laughs, a tired laugh, and sends the cage to be broken up for firewood.

fail.log: The king has you beaten in the courtyard and sends someone else. The someone else comes back with an empty cage too. (-12 health)

events.text: The king who wanted the beast caged is dead, and a carved stone has gone up at the mouth of a cave in the north saying that the beast's cave belongs to the royal house, and that the beast came to the late king. You are asked to write the inscription for the second face of the stone.

choices.text: Write the truth

effects.log: You write: it was sought with a cage, and it did not come. The new king reads it, and is quiet, and has it carved. People come from all over to read the stone with two faces, one a boast and one an apology. The beast, the cave-keepers say, now lies in the sun before it.

choices.text: Write something beautiful and empty

effects.log: You write four lines about virtue and the heavens. They are carved. They are very fine. Nobody reads them twice.

events.text: You are on the far bank of a frozen river with a company of soldiers, and your orders are to stop the refugees crossing: no one from the rebel province is to enter this one. The column is already on the ice. The ice is cracking. And walking ahead of the column, where the cracks run, is a slender beast with pale flames round its hooves, and where it steps the ice goes whole again.

choices.text: Lower your bow, and tell your squad to lower theirs

ok.log: You lower it. Your squad looks at you, and at the beast, and lowers theirs. Then the whole bank does. The column comes over, three hundred people, and the beast brings up the rear, and steps off the ice last, and the river cracks from bank to bank behind it.

fail.log: You lower your bow and your captain strikes you down for it. But the beast stops in the middle of the river and looks at the bank, and every arrow loosed falls short into the snow, and the column crosses anyway. (-8 health)

choices.text: Go down onto the ice and help them across

effects.log: You drop your bow and go down onto the ice. You carry two children and an old man. The beast walks beside you, close enough to touch, and the ice holds under you because it is holding. Your captain never forgives you. You never need him to. (-5 health)

choices.text: Obey your orders

effects.log: You loose with the others. The arrows go up and come down and not one lands among the refugees, as if the air above the river had been folded. The column crosses. You do not know whether to be ashamed or relieved, and you are both, for a long time.

events.text: In a town far from the river, a stranger stops you in the street: one of the refugees from the ice, grown old. "You were on the bank," they say. "I remember every face on that bank."

choices.text: Ask what they remember of yours

effects.log: They tell you, exactly, what your face did that day. It is not what you remember. It is better. Or worse. You walk on carrying it.

choices.text: Ask about the beast

effects.log: "It walked next to my mother," the old refugee says. "The whole way. She said its flank was warm. She said it was the only warm thing in that whole winter."

events.text: A demonic cult has taken a hill village and is making an example of it, a family an hour, and it is not for ransom. They have sent word to the mountains: the five-coloured beast must come and kill one of them with its horn, or the village dies. A beast that kills once is a weapon. You are on a roof above the square. The beast is at the edge of the firelight, and it has not moved.
events.arc: The Cult That Wants a Killing

choices.text: Go down into the square yourself

ok.log: You come down off the roof into the middle of them. It is a long, ugly fight, and you win it, and the village lives. When it is over the beast walks into the square and goes from villager to villager, touching each with the soft tip of its horn, and they stop shaking. It does not look at the cultists on the ground. It does not look at you either. You understand that too.

fail.log: You come down and there are too many. They have you on your knees with the villagers. And then the beast walks into the square and lies down in the middle of it, with its throat bare, and the cultists, confused, gather round it with their knives and their hate, and in the time that takes, the village runs. So do you. (-22 health)

choices.text: Slip round and free the villagers from behind

ok.log: While every cultist is watching the beast at the edge of the firelight, you cut ropes in the dark behind them. By the time they turn round, the square is empty of villagers. The beast turns and walks into the trees, and the cult follows it all night through the mountains, uselessly, and never catches it.

fail.log: You free half of them before you are seen. It is a bad night. The other half, by morning, have been let go, because the cult could not bear the beast's look any longer. (-12 health)

choices.text: Shout to the beast to do it: one life for a village

effects.log: You shout it. The beast turns its head and looks up at your roof. It does not move. Something in its look makes you climb down and go to the square yourself, because the shout was yours and the arithmetic was yours, and so the cost had better be yours too.

events.text: A survivor of the hill village comes to find you years later: the cult has a new temple, and in it, they say, the cultists have painted the five-coloured beast with a bloody horn, to tell everyone it killed for them in the end.
events.arc: The Cult That Wants a Killing

choices.text: Go and paint over it

ok.log: You go in at night and paint over the bloody horn with plain white lime, so that it is only a beast again, with a soft pale tip. The cult paints it red again. You paint it white again. After the fourth time they give up and leave the temple to the bats.

fail.log: You are caught halfway. But the half you painted is the horn, and it stays white, because no cultist will go near it afterward. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell everyone the truth in every inn you pass

effects.log: You tell it everywhere: the square, the throat bared, the village running. The story outruns the painting. In a few years nobody believes the temple, and children in the hill villages play a game called Lie Down in the Square.

events.text: You fought on this field, years ago, and you have never been able to sleep a whole night since. Now there is a young shaman in white walking the cairns with a little bell, laying the dead down, and the villagers say the shaman was born the night a five-coloured beast stood at the gate with a white ribbon on its horn. The shaman stops in front of you and says, "Some of them are still holding on to you."

choices.text: Ask the shaman to lay them down

effects.log: The shaman rings the bell over you and says their names, the ones you killed, the ones you could not save. You did not know the shaman knew them. One by one, something lets go of your shoulders. That night you sleep until noon, and wake crying, and feel lighter than you have since you were young.

choices.text: Say they are yours to carry

effects.log: "Then carry them gently," the shaman says, not arguing, and rings the bell once, softly, near your ear. They are still there. But they are quieter, and you find you can talk to them now.

events.text: A demonic sect wants the white-robed shaman: anyone who can lay the dead down can raise them, they say. You hear that they are on the road to the battlefield of cairns.

choices.text: Stand on the road

ok.log: You stand on the road and they do not pass. When you walk back to the cairns, the shaman is ringing the little bell, and a slender beast is lying among the graves beside the shaman, as if it had been there all along, as if it had known you would come.

fail.log: You stand on the road and they go over you. But when they reach the cairns, the dead rise up, not for them, against them, a field of pale shapes standing between the shaman and the sect, and the sect flees. You never find out if the shaman asked the dead, or the dead decided. (-18 health)

choices.text: Warn the shaman and help them hide

effects.log: You get there first and take the shaman over the hills to a monastery. On the way the shaman rings the bell at every grave you pass, unhurried. At the monastery gate a slender beast is waiting, with a white ribbon on its horn, and the shaman walks in past it like someone coming home.

events.text: You command the left wing of a great army, and the battle is set for dawn. At first light, in the empty middle of the plain between the two lines, a slender beast in five-coloured scales is standing alone. It walked there in the night. It is not moving. The archers of both armies have it in their sights, and nobody has given the order, and nobody will give the order, and nobody can advance without going round it, and nobody wants to be the one who goes round it.

choices.text: Lower your banner first

effects.log: You take your wing's banner from the bearer and lower it till its tip touches the grass. The whole plain watches you do it. After a long time, a banner on the far side goes down too, and then another. By noon both armies are sitting on the grass eating their rations, looking at the beast, and the generals are shouting at each other in a tent, which is how peace begins.

choices.text: Ride out to it alone

ok.log: You ride out into the middle of the plain and dismount beside it. On the far side, the enemy general does the same. The three of you stand there, two generals and a beast, for most of the day. You do not remember afterward what was said. The armies go home.

fail.log: You ride out and an archer on the far side, too young and too frightened, looses at you. The arrow takes you in the shoulder. The beast steps between you and the next one. The archer drops the bow and runs, and it is all over before it starts. (-10 health)

choices.text: Hold your line, and wait for the other side to blink

effects.log: You hold. They hold. The beast holds, all day, all night, all the next day. On the third morning both armies are so tired of standing that they go home by agreement. You never decide whether you lost or won.

events.text: The general who faced you across the plain where the beast stood has come to visit, old now, both of you old. You sit under your plum tree and drink and do not talk about the war you did not fight.

choices.text: Talk about it after all
