effects.log: Halfway down the second jar the old general says, "I was going to give the order. Then I saw your banner go down." You say, "I was going to give the order. Then I saw it standing there." You both laugh until you cough. The field, you hear, has never been ploughed since; nobody will put a blade in it.

choices.text: Plant a second plum tree together

effects.log: You plant a second plum tree beside the first, the two of you, with your old soldier's hands. It flowers the spring after the general dies. You sit under it and think that it is a better monument than a battle.

events.text: {npc}, a grand prince, younger brother of a weak king, has asked you to a private room at night. Your strength is the kind that decides thrones. On {npc}'s robe, over the heart, is the gold-woven badge of the grand princes: a five-coloured beast with one soft horn. {npc} has a list of names, and a date, and wants your sword. "My brother is a fool," {npc} says. "I would be a good king." {npc}'s hand keeps going to the badge, as if it itched.

choices.text: Refuse, and tell {npc} to look at the badge

effects.log: "You are wearing the beast that waits," you say. "That is what it is for. Princes wear it, not kings." {npc} looks down at the badge for a long time. The list goes into the brazier. You hear, the next year, that {npc} has become the king's most loyal minister, and that the king is less of a fool for it.

choices.text: Agree, to keep {npc} close and the plot slow

ok.log: You agree, and then delay, and delay, and find a reason, and another. A year passes. Two. One night {npc} comes to your door without the list and says, "You were never going to, were you?" "No," you say. {npc} laughs, the first real laugh you have heard, and thanks you.

fail.log: {npc} sees through you within a month. You are attacked on a dark road by men with no badges. You live. The plot falls apart without you. (-12 health)

choices.text: Tell the king

effects.log: You tell the king. {npc} is exiled to an island. You did the lawful thing. On the island, you hear, {npc} still wears the badge every day, over the heart, and looks at the sea.

events.text: {npc}, the grand prince who once had a list of names, is dead, never king. The family asks you, as an old friend of the house, to choose what goes into the grave.

choices.text: The robe with the badge, over the heart

effects.log: You lay the robe with the gold-woven badge on {npc}'s chest yourself. The embroidered beast catches the lamplight. You think: it did its work. Some day, centuries on, someone will open this grave and find the badge still bright, and not know what it held back.

choices.text: The list of names, burned, its ash in a little jar

effects.log: You find the ash of the list in an old jar in {npc}'s study; {npc} kept it all those years. You put it in the grave. Whoever finds it will not know what it was. That is the point.

events.text: A warlord has sworn to put a city to the sword at dawn: every soul, for an insult to his name. You are strong enough to stop him, if you go into his camp tonight and kill him. You are on a hill above the camp, and beside you, come out of nowhere, is a five-coloured beast with a soft-tipped horn, looking at the city. It could stop him too. It would have to strike. You understand, without words, that it is asking whether it should be the one, so that you do not have to be.

choices.text: Tell it no: this one is yours

ok.log: You go down into the camp alone. In the morning the warlord is dead and the siege is breaking up, and the city does not know how close it came. When you climb the hill again the beast is still there. It touches the soft tip of its horn to your bloody hands, very lightly, and goes. It never had to strike. You did it for it.

fail.log: You go down into the camp and it nearly kills you. But you get to the warlord's tent and you finish it. You crawl back up the hill at dawn. The beast is lying there waiting for you, and you lie against its warm side until the sun is up and the siege fires go out one by one. (-25 health)

choices.text: Try to end it without a death

ok.log: You walk into the warlord's tent unarmed and talk until dawn. You do not know what does it in the end: your strength, your words, or what is standing on the hill behind you in the first light, which the warlord keeps looking past you at. The siege lifts. Nobody dies. You are more tired than after any fight.

fail.log: You talk and the warlord laughs and throws you out with a spear in your side, and you lie in the mud outside the camp, and dawn comes. And the city does not burn. You find out why at noon: the warlord's own captains would not give the order, because something was standing on the hill. (-15 health)

choices.text: Let it decide

effects.log: You step back. The beast stands on the hill all night, looking at the city. Before dawn it goes down the hill toward the camp, slowly, and you do not follow. At sunrise the siege lifts. Nobody will ever tell you what it did. But for the rest of your life, when you see a plain roe deer in the hills, you look for a long time.

events.text: Years after the siege, in the hills above the city that did not burn, you meet a roe deer. Only a deer. But it has a small round scar on its forehead where a horn might once have been, and it does not run from you, and its eyes are far too old for it.

choices.text: Sit down with it for a while

effects.log: You sit in the grass. It grazes near you, unhurried, careful of the clover, and once it lifts its head and looks at you, and there is no grief in it at all. When you go, you leave the city's name carved on a stone at the spot, and nothing else.

choices.text: Ask it, aloud, whether it was worth it

effects.log: It looks at you, and then down the hill at the city, its roofs, its smoke, its children's kites. Then it goes back to grazing. That is the answer, and you are not big enough for it.

events.text: Something has asked for you by name: a messenger, half bird and half light, comes to your mountain and says that the Four Spirits will seat the five-coloured beast tonight, and that a human who stands at the top of the world must witness it, and that the beast asked for you. You never fought it, the messenger says. That is why.
events.arc: The Witness at the Top of the World

choices.text: Go, and witness

effects.log: You stand on the highest peak at midnight and watch it go up on the clouds, five colours and no grey, slow as smoke, until it is a light among other lights: one like a tortoise, one like a bird of flame, one like a coiled green river of stars. It looks back once, down at you. You are the only human in the world who sees that. You do not tell anyone. You find, after, that you cannot raise your hand in anger for a whole year.

choices.text: Ask the messenger why a beast that never fought deserves a seat

effects.log: "Ask yourself," the messenger says, "how many fights you won, and how many of them ended anything." You think about it for the rest of the night, and go up the mountain at dawn too late to see it rise, and are not sorry, because you have the question instead.

events.text: A young master, very strong, comes up your mountain to ask how you got so far. You find yourself, to your own surprise, about to tell them about a beast that never fought.
events.arc: The Witness at the Top of the World

choices.text: Tell them

effects.log: You tell it all: the clouds, the colours, the seat. The young master listens with the polite face of someone who came for a sword technique. Then, at the end, the face changes. They go down the mountain slowly. You hear, years later, that they have never killed anyone.

choices.text: Teach them a technique instead

effects.log: You teach them a good technique. They go away happy. You stand on the peak afterward and feel that you have given a child a knife when it asked for bread, and resolve to do better with the next.

events.text: In an old northern capital, below a cliff with a pavilion on it, above white rapids, there is a cave the locals call the Qilin Cave, and before it a flat stone with great hoofprints worn into it. The story is that the first king of an ancient kingdom kept a qilin-horse in the cave, and at the end of his reign rode it up from that stone into heaven, and never came back.

choices.text: Put your hand in one of the prints

effects.log: Your hand fits a print with room to spare. The stone is warm, though the night is cold. From inside the cave, very faintly, you hear something breathe, small and slow, like a foal asleep in straw. You take your hand away and go up to the pavilion quietly so as not to wake it.

choices.text: Climb to the pavilion and read the old poems

effects.log: The pavilion walls are written over with poems by travellers. One, very old, says: the city is empty, there is a sliver of moon; the qilin-horse went and did not return; where does the heavenly grandson wander? You read it three times. Below, the rapids say the same thing over and over in a language that has no words.

events.text: You come back to the stone before the Qilin Cave years later, at night, without meaning to. Your feet brought you. There are footprints in the frost on the stone: small, cloven, careful, going round and round the great old prints and setting one hoof, just one, inside the biggest.

choices.text: Wait by the cave mouth till dawn

effects.log: You wait. At first light a young beast comes out of the cave, roe-sized, grey-gold, with a bud of a horn, and goes to the stone, and puts its hoof in the great print, and looks up at the sky for a long time. Then it sees you. It does not run. You feel that you are watching someone measure themselves against a parent, and you look away, out of courtesy.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of dew on the stone

effects.log: You leave a bowl, filled from the leaves, and go. In the morning the bowl is empty and set upside down, neatly, beside the great prints, the way a child returns a bowl to a neighbour.

events.text: You are the strongest jailer the provincial prison has ever had, the one they bring in when a prisoner will not talk. The new magistrate, a young one born in this very prison to a prisoner mother, they say on the night a five-coloured beast stood outside the walls, has called you in. "I am told you are good at your work," the magistrate says. "From today you will not do it."

choices.text: Ask the magistrate how confessions will be had

effects.log: "By finding out what happened," the magistrate says, "instead of what someone will say to make you stop." It takes you a year to understand that sentence. In that year the magistrate frees eleven people you broke, and you carry the instruments out to the gate and stack them there with your own hands.

choices.text: Lay your tools down on the floor at once

effects.log: You lay them down. Your hands shake. The magistrate looks at your hands, and at the tools, and says, "Good. Now you will help me find the ones you hurt." It takes ten years. Some of them spit at you. Some of them do not.

choices.text: Tell the magistrate the province will not stand for it

effects.log: "Then the province will have to sit," the magistrate says. A month later a noble's hired killers come for the magistrate in the night, and you find yourself, to your own astonishment, standing in the corridor between them and the magistrate's door.

events.text: The magistrate who ended the cruel questioning in the province is very old, and dying, in the courtroom itself, on a mat, because the magistrate wanted to die where the work was. You are old too. The courtyard gate is open, and in it, very still, is a beast with a faded black ribbon on its horn.

choices.text: Bring it in to the magistrate

effects.log: It comes in at your side, past the stacked rusting tools by the gate, and lays its head by the magistrate's hand. The magistrate unties the black ribbon, and its scales along the flank darken, deep and clear as ink, and stay. "I was born the night it stood at the prison wall," the magistrate whispers to you. "Did you know?" You did not. You are glad to know now.

choices.text: Stay at the door and keep the curious away

effects.log: You stand in the door, broad as ever, and keep the crowd back while the beast goes in. You hear the magistrate laugh once, softly. When it comes out, its flank is darker, and it touches your old jailer's hands with the soft tip of its horn, as if they were worth touching.

events.text: You are an Earth Immortal newly come up, and the Jade court has made you an envoy's clerk for the audit of the spirits. The tortoise has produced its shell, the dragon a rain. The five-coloured beast has produced, on the bare cloud floor before your lectern, one blade of grass, standing straight. The envoy wants to know how you will enter it in the ledger.

choices.text: Enter it as: a thousand years, one blade, unbent

effects.log: You write it, exactly so. The envoy reads it over your shoulder and says nothing for a long time. Then the envoy initials it, and the beast, which had been watching your brush, lies down on the cloud beside its blade of grass and closes its eyes.

choices.text: Ask the envoy how one audits a thing that did nothing

effects.log: "Carefully," the envoy says. "It is the hardest kind of thing to audit. Everyone who did something has a record. It has only an absence: every war it was not in, every blow it did not strike." You spend a century learning to read absences. It is the best work you ever do.

events.text: The blade of grass from the audit has been kept in the Jade court's archive under glassy jade. A clerk of the archive tells you it has never wilted in all that time, and that someone keeps trying to steal it.

choices.text: Find out who

ok.log: It is an old immortal who was a warlord, once, below, and who cannot bear that something so small outweighed every battle. You do not report them. You take them to see the grass, and sit with them, and after a while they stop trying.

fail.log: You never find out. But the grass is never taken, either, because now you visit it every day.

choices.text: Leave it: let whoever it is have it

effects.log: The grass goes missing a month later. Nobody minds as much as they expected to. You hear rumours of a blade of grass growing on a cloud somewhere, unbent, and an old warlord-immortal sitting by it every day.

events.text: The Four Spirits have sent for you to testify. Once, below, in your mortal life, you crossed paths with the five-coloured beast. They want to know one thing: in all the time you knew of it, did it ever bend the grass?

choices.text: Tell the truth, all of it, even what you are not sure of

effects.log: You tell them everything, including the one thing you were never sure of: a fawn that ran from it into a ravine, long ago. The council is quiet. Then a voice like a temple bell says from somewhere behind you, "Yes. That one. I went back." The council writes something. You are thanked, and sent out, and you never learn what they decided, only that the seat is not empty.

choices.text: Say only what you saw with your own eyes

effects.log: You say what you saw. It is not much. The council thanks you, and you understand from their faces that most witnesses have said far more, and far less truly, and that your little is worth a great deal.

choices.text: Ask why a beast must be perfect to sit with them

effects.log: The council is silent a long time. Then the eldest voice says, "It need not be perfect. It need only have gone back, every time." You think of all the things in your own long life you never went back to mend, and go out of the hall resolved.

events.text: A heavenly immortal stops you on a cloud road: the grandchild, many times over, of the first child the five-coloured beast heralded with a ribbon. They heard you testified. "Was it true," they ask, "that my ancestor's mother tied the ribbon herself? With her own hands?"

choices.text: Tell them what you know of it

effects.log: You tell them the story as you have heard it: the gate, the ants, the two nights, the faded red ribbon off a sewing basket. They listen as if to a lullaby. At the end they say, "That was my family's whole fortune. A ribbon." "Yes," you say. "It was enough."

choices.text: Tell them to ask the beast

effects.log: They do. You hear it took the beast a whole afternoon to answer, lying on a cloud with its chin on its forelegs, telling it slowly, as if it were the best story it knew.

events.text: You are an Immortal Sovereign, and the Great Peace has asked to speak with you. Not a beast any more: a stillness in the shape of one, vast and faint, lying across the dawn over a whole world. "There is a world," it says, in a voice like every temple bell at once, "that has never had a single quiet year. Not one. I cannot go there; I would be only a rumour. Will you carry me?"

choices.text: Carry it, and go down into that world

effects.log: You go down into a world of endless war carrying nothing anyone can see. You do not fight. You stand in places. Where you stand, hands do not rise. It takes three hundred years. On the morning of the first quiet year, the whole world wakes up not knowing why it slept so well, and you sit down in a field and weep like a child.

choices.text: Ask why it cannot go itself

effects.log: "Because peace that comes from the sky is a miracle," it says, "and miracles end. Peace that a person carries in on their own feet is a habit. Habits last." You think about this for a long time, and then you go.

choices.text: Refuse: you have fought too much to be the one

effects.log: "That," it says, gently, "is why it should be you." You still refuse. It does not argue. But every dawn after, it lies across your sky, patient, and you find that you are thinking about that world more and more.

events.text: Long after the world of endless war learned its first quiet year, a child of that world comes up into the Upper Realm, the first of them ever to rise. They have been told the story of the one who came down and stood in places. They want to see your hands.

choices.text: Show them

effects.log: You hold them out. They are old hands, scarred from a hundred thousand fights before you went down. The child looks at them a long time and then says, "They are only hands." "Yes," you say. "That was the whole secret."

choices.text: Show them the field where you sat down

effects.log: You take them down to the field, which is a meadow now that no one mows. The child sits down in it where you sat. You leave them there. Some things a person has to find by sitting in them.

events.text: An Immortal Sovereign of the Upper Realm, vain and very old, has had a cage of gold made and set before the throne, and wants you to fill it. "The five-coloured beast comes only to the virtuous," the Sovereign says. "Bring it. Let every court see that it came to me."

choices.text: Refuse

effects.log: "If it is in a cage," you say, "it did not come to you." The Sovereign's face does not change. You are not invited to that court again for five hundred years, which in the Upper Realm is a fairly mild rebuke, and you are glad of the quiet.

choices.text: Go and ask the beast, and bring back its answer

ok.log: You find it lying on a cloud above a valley at war, watching. You tell it. It gets up and comes with you, to your horror, all the way to the throne hall, and walks into the golden cage, and lies down. The court gasps. Then it walks out again, through the bars, as if they were mist. It looks at the Sovereign for a long moment and leaves. The cage is melted down the next day.

fail.log: You cannot find it anywhere in the Upper Realm. You come back and say so. The Sovereign is displeased. That night you dream of a beast lying on a cloud, watching a war below, and you understand it was busy.

events.text: The vain Sovereign who wanted a beast in a cage of gold has fallen from the throne: a war in heaven, the kind that happens once an age. In the ruins of the throne hall you find the golden cage again, bent, and in it, asleep, a small grey bird with a broken wing.

choices.text: Open the cage and mend the wing

effects.log: You open the cage and splint the wing with a sliver of jade. The bird flies, in a month. You leave the cage door open behind it. Somewhere, you feel, something five-coloured nods.

choices.text: Leave the bird where it is safe

effects.log: You leave it. The cage is the only shelter in the ruins. You bring it seed every day until the wing heals and it leaves through the bent bars on its own. You think: a cage is only a cage when the door will not open.

events.text: A hard year: a sect war in the next province, villages burned, bandits on the roads. In the market an omen-reader is shouting that a five-coloured beast was seen on the hill at dusk, and that a qilin seen in a bad age means a great death is coming, and the crowd is talking about going up the hill with spears to kill the omen before it comes true.

choices.text: Tell the crowd it comes for births as well as deaths

ok.log: "It comes at births too," you say, loudly. "Who in this town is with child?" Half the crowd turns to look at a baker's wife, who goes scarlet, and the talk turns to cradles, and nobody goes up the hill.

fail.log: They shout you down. But you walk up the hill ahead of them in the dark, and when they come with their spears there is nothing there but a few careful hoofprints going round a sleeping hare. (-4 health)

choices.text: Say nothing: it can look after itself

effects.log: You say nothing. They go up with spears and come back with nothing and feel foolish. In a hard age, you think, being hunted for being seen is what it gets. You wonder how it bears it.

events.text: You have been set to guard a royal tomb workshop while a dead king's grave goods are made. A painter is working on the mudguard flaps for the king's saddle, layered birch bark, painting a heavenly horse galloping on clouds. The painter keeps going out at dawn to sketch something in the pine wood. On the flap, on the horse's forehead, there is a curve that might be a tuft of mane, or might be a horn.

choices.text: Ask the painter what is in the pine wood

effects.log: "A horse," the painter says firmly. Then, more quietly: "It stood for me. Every morning. It let me call it a horse. I think it was being kind." The painter adds one more stroke to the curve on the forehead and will not say whether it is mane.

choices.text: Go out to the pine wood at dawn yourself

ok.log: There is a beast standing in the clearing, very still, in the pose of the horse on the flap. It sees you and holds the pose anyway, patiently, because the painter is not finished. You back away and say nothing to anyone.

fail.log: You get lost among the pines and come back muddy. The painter has finished the flap. The curve on the forehead is very clear now, and you still cannot tell what it is. (-3 health)

events.text: A scholar of antiquities has an old saddle flap of layered birch bark laid out on a table, from a king's grave, and is arguing with another scholar over the curve on the painted horse's forehead: a horn, or a tuft of mane? They want your opinion, because you are standing there.

choices.text: Say: a horn

effects.log: "A horn," you say. One scholar crows. The other sulks. You do not know why you were so sure. The flap, under the lamp, seems to look at you, pleased, and a little alarmed.

choices.text: Say: a horse, as the painter called it

effects.log: "The painter called it a horse," you say, "so it is a horse." Both scholars stare at you. You feel, absurdly, that you have kept someone's secret, and that they are grateful.

events.text: The last ferry of the day, one place left on it, and two caravans' porters fighting over it with carrying poles. You are waiting too, with your own bundle. Somebody is going to get a split head. Then, from the far bank, through the mist, comes a single sentence in a voice like a temple bell: "The river will still be here in the morning." Everyone stops. Nobody can see who said it.

choices.text: Give up your own place on the ferry

effects.log: You step off. Both caravans get across. You sleep under the ferry shed on the near bank and in the night something warm lies down on the other side of the thin plank wall, and you hear it breathing slowly until dawn.

choices.text: Ask the ferryman who spoke

effects.log: The old ferryman spits in the river. "Every few years," he says. "Always one sentence. Always the right one. My grandfather said it ended a blood feud on this landing once with eight words." He will not say what it is. You think he knows.

events.text: Years after the ferry, you find yourself between two people about to kill each other over something small, and you open your mouth, and want, more than anything, one sentence like the one from the far bank.

choices.text: Say the simplest true thing you can find

ok.log: "Tomorrow you will both still be alive, if you let it," you say. It is not a bell. But it is enough: they stop, and look at you, and then at each other, and someone laughs. You tell the ferryman's grandchild about it later, and the grandchild writes it down.

fail.log: You say it badly and they both turn on you instead. But by the time they have finished shoving you, they have forgotten what they were angry at. That counts. (-6 health)

choices.text: Say nothing and step between them

effects.log: You say nothing. You simply stand there, between them, the way it stood between the bank and the ferry. Neither of them can get round you without looking foolish. In the end neither tries.

events.text: The crown prince's procession goes by on the palace road, and at its head the one banner that never goes before the king: yellow silk, three bearers to hold it steady in the wind, painted with a gentle scaled beast with one soft horn. You are a general of the heir's faction. The king is old and cruel. The heir is a sage, everyone says, born on a night a five-coloured beast stood at the palace gate. The faction wants the heir to take the throne now, by the sword, and you are the sword.

choices.text: Go to the heir and offer the throne

effects.log: The heir hears you out in a quiet room and then says, "Look at the banner they carry before me. It is the beast that waits. If I seize, they will have to take it down." You are dismissed, kindly. You go away and think about banners.

choices.text: Tell the faction the heir must wait

ok.log: You tell them, and because you are the sword, they listen. The faction grumbles and waits. The old king lives eleven more cruel years. The heir is crowned without a drop of blood, and the banner is folded away in blue cotton and kept.

fail.log: They call you a coward and try it without you, and it fails, and the heir is nearly lost in the purge that follows. But the heir does not fall, and does not seize, and waits. (-10 health)

events.text: The heir who waited is king at last, and old already. You are old too. The new king sends for you and shows you the folded yellow banner with the scaled beast on it. "I wish to give it to my own heir," the king says, "and I wish you to carry it the first time, because you were the sword that did not cut."

choices.text: Carry it

effects.log: You carry it at the grip, with two young bearers on the cords, down the palace road in the wind. Your arms shake. At the end of the road, among the crowd, very still, there is something with five-coloured scales, watching its own picture go by. You do not drop the banner.

choices.text: Tell the king to give it to someone young

effects.log: "Give it to the young," you say. "I carried the waiting. Let them carry it now." The king laughs and agrees, and you watch from the crowd, and someone in the crowd beside you is not a person at all, and you do not look, out of courtesy.

events.text: You are guarding the painters in a great king's tomb while they work: smooth granite walls, oil lamps, the four guardians going up on the four walls in strong colours. The master painter lies on a plank under the ceiling stones, painting immortals and lotus, and keeps leaving a space empty. "For the gentle one," the master says. "It has promised to come and stand for me."

choices.text: Hold the lamp for the master all night

effects.log: You hold the lamp until your arm is numb. Near dawn there is a sound of soft hooves on the stone floor of the passage, and the master says "Ah," and paints fast, and you keep your eyes on the lamp flame because you have been told to and because you are afraid of what looking would cost. When the master climbs down, the space is filled.

choices.text: Ask the master why it should be on the ceiling and not a wall

effects.log: "The walls are for the guardians," the master says. "They face out, against things. The ceiling is for the ones who face in, toward the sleeper. It never faces against anything." You think about that all night.

events.text: The tomb is sealed. You were the last guard out. Years later you wake in the night certain that somewhere under the earth, in the dark, a painted beast on a ceiling has just looked down at the sleeper, and that the sleeper is not alone.

choices.text: Go and stand at the mound

effects.log: You stand at the grassy mound until dawn. You hear nothing. But the grass on the mound is the tallest and straightest you have ever seen, and nobody has ever mown it.

choices.text: Light a lamp in your own room and leave it burning

effects.log: You light a lamp and leave it burning till morning, for a painter long dead and a sleeper you never saw and a beast on a ceiling. It seems the least you can do. It seems to be enough.

events.text: You lead a troop of cavalry down the only road into a valley where, your orders say, a rebel village is to be burned. Halfway down, lying across the road, is a slender beast in five-coloured scales. It is not blocking you in any way a soldier would understand: it is only lying there. To get past, the horses will have to step over it, or on it.

choices.text: Turn the troop round

effects.log: You turn them round. Your orders are broken. The village is not burned, that day or any other. You are reduced to a common trooper for it, and in the long evenings by the fire you find you are happier as one.

choices.text: Order the troop to go round it, through the meadow

effects.log: You take them round through the meadow. The horses will not go. Not one of them. They plant their feet at the meadow's edge and shiver. In the end you sit there till dark, and the orders are changed by a rider in the night.

choices.text: Dismount and speak to it

ok.log: You kneel on the road and ask it, as you would ask an elder, what it wants. It looks at you, and then down the valley, at the smoke of the village's cooking fires, at the children's voices carrying up. You understand. You get back on your horse and take the troop back up the road, and write a report that says the village was empty.

fail.log: You kneel to speak to it and your horse, frightened by your kneeling, kicks you. When you are on your feet again the beast is gone, and the road is clear, and you cannot, for the life of you, bring yourself to ride down it. (-5 health)

events.text: At dawn the temple bell on the mountain rings, and from somewhere in the valley below, something answers it: one long note, low and clean, in perfect tune. The monks stop swinging the striker. Everyone in the valley stops what they are doing.

choices.text: Stand still and listen until it ends

effects.log: You stand still. The note goes on longer than any breath could. When it ends you find you have forgiven someone you had not meant to forgive, and you do not mind.

choices.text: Hum the note back

effects.log: You hum it back, badly. In the valley, after a moment, the note comes again, shorter, as if amused. For the rest of the day you cannot stop humming.

events.text: From a terrace of the Upper Realm you can see the world below when the clouds part. Today, in a valley you knew as a mortal, deer are grazing at the edge of a barley field and the farmers are working beside them, and nobody is chasing anybody. An old immortal beside you says it is the year the five-coloured beast took its seat, and that in a good age, now, the animals do not run.
events.arc: When the Animals Do Not Run

choices.text: Go down to the valley and walk among them

effects.log: You go down in a mortal's shape. A doe lets you walk beside her to the stream. A fox crosses your path and looks up, curious, not afraid. You sit down by the barley field and cry, a little, for every animal you ever saw run from you, and then you stop, because none of them are running now.

choices.text: Ask how long it will last

effects.log: "As long as the age is good," the old immortal says. "So, not forever. So, it is up to them." You watch the deer for the rest of the day and think about how much of it is up to you.

events.text: The clouds part over the same valley many years later. The deer are running again: there is a war. An old farmer in the barley is standing still in the middle of it all, holding out a handful of grain to a fawn that has not decided yet whether to be afraid.
events.arc: When the Animals Do Not Run

choices.text: Send down a quiet year to that one field

effects.log: You can do that much, from up here: one field, one quiet year. The war goes round it like water round a stone. The fawn eats from the farmer's hand. It is not enough. It is not nothing.

choices.text: Only watch

effects.log: You watch. The fawn decides. It comes, slowly, and eats. Nobody in heaven did that. A farmer did, with a handful of grain. You go back inside humbled.

events.text: You go hunting, as your family always has, and in a quiet year the animals will not run. A roe deer looks at you and goes on eating. A pheasant walks round your feet. The old hunters say this happened once in their own grandfathers' time, and nobody believed them.

choices.text: Unstring your bow and sit with them

effects.log: You unstring it and sit on a log. The deer comes closer. You have the strangest feeling that you once sat on a cloud at a round table with a dragon and a bird of fire and a tortoise, and argued for exactly this. You go home with nothing in your bag and a full heart.

choices.text: Hunt anyway: a family must eat

effects.log: You draw on the deer, and it looks at you, and does not run, and your arrow goes wide by an arm's length, and the next, and the next. You go home with nothing, ashamed and not sure why. The next year the animals run again, and you are almost relieved.

events.text: A war comes to the province, and the animals start running again. A fawn, panicked by the drums, runs straight into your arms in the lane and stands there trembling.

choices.text: Carry it back to the forest edge

effects.log: You carry it to the edge of the forest and set it down. It looks back at you once. You say to it, aloud, feeling foolish, "It will be a good age again." You find you are promising it, and that you mean to keep the promise.

choices.text: Keep it in your yard until the war passes

effects.log: It lives in your yard for two years, eating windfall, never once touching your cabbages. When the war ends you open the gate, and it goes, and the next spring there is a doe at the edge of your field with a fawn of her own, and neither of them runs.

events.text: There is a valley where you live now, or that you have come to, where the fences are made of swords: old blades, rusted, stuck point-down in the earth with beans climbing them. Nobody remembers why the war ended. Nobody here, the headman tells you, has raised a hand in anger in living memory. Your own hand, when you are angry, simply does not rise.

choices.text: Plant your own sword in the fence

effects.log: You push it into the earth at the end of the row. A child plants a bean at its foot. By midsummer it is green to the hilt. You have never felt so safe in your life, or so strange, as if you were standing inside someone's long patience.

choices.text: Ask the oldest person why the war ended

effects.log: "It just stopped," the oldest person says. "One morning everyone woke up and could not remember how to hate each other. My grandmother said there was something in the sky that dawn, five colours, lying across the whole valley like a sleeping animal." You look up. There is nothing. You feel looked at anyway.

events.text: A stranger comes into the valley of sword fences with a drawn blade, a murim fighter fleeing some feud, and finds that here the blade will not lift. They stand in the lane, furious and bewildered, while children watch.

choices.text: Take them home and feed them

effects.log: You take them home and feed them rice and soup. They eat like a starving dog, then sleep for two days. On the third they ask, in a small voice, if they can stay. The sword goes into the fence at the end of your row.

choices.text: Explain the valley to them

effects.log: You explain as best you can, which is not well. They leave the next morning, back toward their feud. But they leave the sword behind, stuck in the fence, and you hear years later that they never fought again.

events.text: Below the pavilion above the rapids, before the old cave, the flat stone has two sets of great hoofprints in it now: one worn almost smooth, one sharper, as if made a thousand years later. The guides say a second founder was carried up from here by a second beast. When you put your hand in the sharper print, it fits as if it were your own foot.

choices.text: Stand where the beast stood

effects.log: You stand on the prints. The rapids roar. For a breath you feel a weight on your back, someone dying and trusting you, and the cold air of the climb, and the pull of the sky. Then you are only a traveller standing on a stone at night, and your back aches for no reason for a week.

choices.text: Climb to the pavilion and write a line on the wall

effects.log: You find space among the old poems and write: it went, and it did not come back, and it was not lost. You do not know where the line came from. Under it, in the morning, someone has drawn a small hoofprint in charcoal.

events.text: Someone dying asks to be carried to the stone before the cave: a grandparent, a teacher, an old sworn friend. They want to die with a hand in the hoofprints, they say, because the old stories say the beast still carries people up from there, if they ask nicely.

choices.text: Carry them there on your back

effects.log: It is a long way up the cliff path. At the stone you set them down and put their hand in the sharper print. They smile at something over your shoulder and say, "There you are," and go. You do not look round. You would rather not know; you would rather believe.

choices.text: Tell them the stories are only stories, and stay with them at home

effects.log: You stay with them at home. Near the end they say, "I can hear rapids," though the river is three days away. In the morning there is a small, careful hoofprint in the frost on the threshold.

events.text: In a poor village schoolroom, kept in a cloth on the teacher's desk, there is a book made of thin tablets of jade. The teacher lets each child read one line on their first day. When it is your turn, the jade is cool under your fingers, and as you read, very faintly, you hear a bell.

choices.text: Read the line aloud

effects.log: The line says who you could be. Not who you are: who you could be, if you were brave. Everyone hears it ring. You go red. The teacher writes it down in the register, beside your name, and says, "Now you know. Now it is your problem."

choices.text: Read it silently, and keep it

effects.log: You read it silently. The bell rings only in your head. You never tell anyone what the line said. But for the rest of your life, when you have a choice to make, you hear that bell very faintly, and know which way it means.

events.text: A great sect has sent a master to take the book of jade from the village school for its own library: a treasure, they say, wasted on farm children. The teacher is very old. The master is very strong.

choices.text: Stand in the schoolroom door

ok.log: You stand in the door. The master looks at you, a farmer, and laughs, and then stops laughing, because you will not move and something rings, faintly, behind you. The master goes away. The book stays with the children.

fail.log: The master moves you, easily. But when the master lifts the book from the desk it is only cold green stone, blank, and it stays blank in the sect's library for a hundred years. When it is finally sent back, the first child who reads it hears a bell. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let the master read one line first

effects.log: "Read one line," you say, "like the children do." The master, amused, reads. The bell rings. The master's face changes, and changes again, and then the master sets the book down very carefully and walks out without a word, and does not come back.

events.text: You are old, and you go back to the village school one more time to read the book of jade again. You want to know whether the line has changed.

choices.text: Read it

effects.log: It has not changed. It is the same line. Who you could be. You read it with your old eyes and see that, somehow, without noticing, you became it, or most of it. The bell rings softly, like someone pleased trying not to show it.

choices.text: Let a child read it to you instead

effects.log: A small child reads you their own line, stumbling, and the bell rings, and the child's face lights up. You decide that was better than reading your own.

events.text: An old grave is opened when a road is cut through a hillside, and you are there, by chance or work, when the robe is lifted out: a prince's robe, and over the heart a badge of gold thread, still bright, a gentle scaled beast with a soft horn. When you touch it, your chest goes warm, as if someone had laid a hand there to stop you doing something.

choices.text: Ask that it be put back in the grave

effects.log: They laugh at you, and then, seeing your face, ask why. You cannot say. In the end the robe goes to a temple, not a market, and the badge is kept in a box no one is allowed to sell. That will do.

choices.text: Keep the warmth, and wonder what it stopped

effects.log: For a long time after, whenever you are about to take something that is not yours, a place, a post, a share, your chest goes warm in exactly that spot. You start to think of it as an old friend.

events.text: You have the chance to take something that is not quite yours: a post that should go to someone else, an inheritance a cousin has a better claim to, a rank in a sect. Everyone tells you to take it. Over your heart, the warmth comes.

choices.text: Wait, and let it go to the one it belongs to

effects.log: You let it go. It goes to the cousin, the rival, the other one. They are grateful in a way that embarrasses you both. Ten years later, the thing comes back to you anyway, freely given. You wear it the way a prince wore a badge: over the heart, knowing what it means.

choices.text: Take it, and feel the warmth go cold

effects.log: You take it. The warmth goes out of your chest like a lamp blown out. You have the thing. You do not have the warmth again, not ever, and you know which you would rather.

events.text: You are let into an ancient tomb by a keeper who owes you a favour. On the walls the four guardians are fading, a green dragon, a white tiger, a red bird, a black tortoise. And on the ceiling stones, among immortals and lotus, something faint, gentle, looking down. You lie on the cold floor to see it better, and it is looking at you.

choices.text: Lie there until the lamp burns low

effects.log: You lie there a long time. You feel how it feels to watch one sleeper for a thousand years while your own colours fade: patient, and not lonely, quite. When the keeper calls you out, you are reluctant to leave it alone, and then you remember it is not alone; there is the sleeper.

choices.text: Ask the keeper who painted it

effects.log: "Nobody knows," the keeper says. "The story is the master painter lay on a plank for a whole night waiting for it to come and stand, and it came." The keeper lowers the lamp. "The colour is going. In a hundred years you will not see it at all." "It will still be there," you say, and are surprised how sure you are.

events.text: Tomb robbers have been in the old tomb, the keeper sends word: they chipped at the walls for the pigment, and were found in the morning lying on the floor under the ceiling, unhurt, weeping, unable to say why.

choices.text: Go and sit with the robbers in the jail

effects.log: They tell you, haltingly, that they looked up. That is all. They looked up and something on the ceiling looked back at them as if they were sleepers too, and worth watching over. Two of them become tomb keepers when they are let out.

choices.text: Go and repaint what they chipped

ok.log: You mix the colours carefully, by lamplight, and fill the chips. You do not touch the ceiling. You do not need to. When you finish, you feel, very distinctly, thanked.

fail.log: Your colours are wrong and the patches show. You leave them. They look like scars, and scars are honest. The keeper says the ceiling seems to like them.

events.text: In a sect treasury, or a noble's collection, or a scholar's study, two old experts are arguing over a painted saddle flap of birch bark from a king's grave: is the crescent on the white horse's forehead a horn or a tuft of mane? It has been going on for three days. You know the answer. You do not know how you know.

choices.text: Say nothing, and smile

effects.log: You say nothing. They argue for three more days. You find it the funniest thing you have ever witnessed, and cannot explain why to anyone, and laugh in your sleep for a week.

choices.text: Tell them: a horn, but it wanted to be called a horse

effects.log: They stare at you. "Wanted?" one says. "Wanted," you say firmly, and leave. You hear they now argue about that instead, which seems to you an improvement.

events.text: A painter asks you to sit for a portrait. Halfway through, the painter stops and says, "You have the strangest way of holding still. Like an animal being patient for a painter it likes."

choices.text: Ask the painter to call you something you are not

effects.log: "Paint me as a merchant," you say, "or a fisher. Anything." The painter laughs, and does, and the portrait is very good and looks nothing like you. You hang it in your hall and feel, looking at it, wonderfully free.

choices.text: Hold still and say nothing

effects.log: You hold still. The painter paints you exactly. In the finished picture there is something odd about your forehead, a little curve of light there, that the painter cannot explain and will not paint out.

events.text: There is a walled town in the south whose peak, above it, is shaped like a deer lying down with its legs folded under it. The moon rises over the peak's back every night, and people come from far away to see it. The town has had no war in five hundred years. When you see the peak for the first time you have to sit down on the road.

choices.text: Climb the peak at night

effects.log: You climb in the dark and sit on the summit as the moon comes up behind you. The rock is warm. The rock is breathing, very slowly, once an hour perhaps. You lie down along the ridge with your cheek on the stone and fall asleep, and wake at dawn rested as you have never been.

choices.text: Watch the moonrise from the town wall with everyone else

effects.log: You stand on the wall with the townspeople as the moon spills over the peak. An old man beside you says the peak is a sleeping beast that keeps the town. Everyone says that; nobody believes it; everyone believes it. You find you are smiling at the peak as if at an old friend's face.

events.text: An army is marching on the walled town below the peak shaped like a lying deer. The townspeople are not afraid. They say it has happened before. You are not so sure.

choices.text: Stand on the wall with them at moonrise

effects.log: The moon comes up over the peak's back, and in its light the army on the plain halts, and stares at the mountain, and cannot for some reason go on. By morning it has turned aside to the west. The townspeople go back to bed, unsurprised. You stay on the wall till dawn, thanking a mountain.

choices.text: Ride out to meet the army's general

ok.log: You ride out and ask the general to look up at the peak at moonrise before deciding. The general, humouring you, does. The army turns west in the morning. The general does not explain, and does not need to.

fail.log: The general has you thrown out of camp. But that night the moon rises over the peak and the army will not march. (-8 health)

events.text: There is a field on the great plain that is never mown and that no army will cross: they march a day out of their way to go round it. At its edge, old spears are rusting where they were thrown down, and two banners from two kingdoms stand side by side, lowered. You stand at the edge. You cannot make yourself step in. Your chest hurts as if a great many hooves had gone over it.

choices.text: Kneel at the edge and put your hand on the grass

effects.log: The grass is cool and stands straight under your palm. You feel the weight of a charge, and the not-moving, and then the quiet after, which went on, and on, and became a peace. You stay till dark. When you stand, your chest no longer hurts.

choices.text: Ask a herder why no army will cross it

effects.log: "Something fell there," the herder says, "and did not get up, and did not fight back. The two kings made peace at the edge the next day. Nobody wants to walk over that." The herder looks at you. "You look like you know."

events.text: A young general, ambitious, has ordered the cavalry straight across the unmown field to save a day's march. You are riding with them, or watching from a hill, or standing in their way.

choices.text: Ride ahead and stop at the field's edge

ok.log: You rein in at the edge and turn your horse to face the column. The general rides up, shouting. Then the general looks past you at the grass, and goes quiet, and turns the whole column aside. Nobody ever crosses that field.

fail.log: They ride you down. And then, at the field's edge, every horse in the column stops dead, rears, and will not go on. They go round. You are carried home on a door, and do not regret it. (-12 health)

choices.text: Let them try

effects.log: They try. The horses will not step onto the grass. Not one. The general beats the lead horse until a sergeant takes the whip away. They go round, a day late, and the general never tries again.

events.text: In the hills above a city that was once nearly put to the sword, there is an old roe deer the herders will not hunt. It has a small round scar on its forehead where a horn might have been. It does not run from people. When it looks at you, you feel that you owe a city something, and that the city owes you, and that the debts cancelled long ago.

choices.text: Bring it windfall chestnuts

effects.log: You bring chestnuts every autumn. It eats only the ones that fell; it will not touch the ones you knocked down. You understand that it once was something that cared very much about that, and still does, horn or no horn.

choices.text: Sit by it and look down at the city

effects.log: You sit together on the hillside and watch the cooking smoke come up from the city, thousands of hearths. It is a plain deer. It is also, you are certain, the reason all that smoke is cooking smoke. You feel a horn's ache in your own forehead, and then it passes.

events.text: The old roe deer of the hills is dying, lying in the grass above the city. The herders have come to watch, at a distance, holding their caps.

choices.text: Go and sit beside it at the end

effects.log: You sit beside it. At the very end it lifts its head toward the city, and for one breath its coat flickers, blue, red, yellow, white, black, and then it is only a deer again, and still. The herders bury it on the hill. Nobody in the city below knows. You decide that is how it wanted it.

choices.text: Go down and tell the city

ok.log: You tell them. Most do not believe you. But some come up the hill, a few dozen, with lamps, and stand round the deer in the dark until it is gone. It seems to be enough company.

fail.log: They laugh at you. You go back up the hill alone, and sit with it, and that is all right too.

events.text: Above the rapids there is a cave mouth overgrown with vines, and in winter the snow lies before it smooth and untouched, as if nothing had gone in or out for a hundred years. You have come a long way to see it and you do not know why. You cannot bring yourself to leave a footprint in that snow.

choices.text: Call softly into the cave

effects.log: You call, softly, the way you would wake a sleeper you loved. Nothing answers. But the vines over the cave mouth stir, though there is no wind, and you feel, very distinctly, that you are being told: not yet. Not in an age like this.

choices.text: Leave without a footprint

effects.log: You turn back on your own tracks, stepping in each one exactly. It takes a long time. When you reach the road you look back, and the snow before the cave is still perfect, and you feel you have done the only kind thing there was to do.

events.text: A child of the village below the rapids asks you why no great omens ever come any more: no beasts at births, no signs of good kings, nothing, the way there was in the old stories.

choices.text: Tell the child: make an age worth coming out for

effects.log: "It is waiting," you say, "for an age worth coming out for. That part is up to us." The child thinks about this seriously, and then goes and stops two other children fighting. It is a start. Up above the rapids, the snow before the cave is still smooth, but it is a start.

choices.text: Tell the child the old stories were only stories

effects.log: The child is disappointed. So, you find, are you. That night you dream of a cave mouth and a breath of warm hay from inside it, and wake with your face wet.

events.text: You are reading an old chronicle of a dead kingdom, year by year, and it ends abruptly: in the west, at a hunt, a strange beast was taken. Nothing more. Pressed between the last pages is a faded embroidered ribbon. You find that you have turned back your sleeve to wipe your face, and that your sleeve is wet.

choices.text: Keep the ribbon

effects.log: You keep it, folded, in your sleeve. You never learn whose it was. But you find that you cannot stand to watch any creature hunted that nobody can name, and you go out of your way, all your life, to stop it.

choices.text: Write one more line in the chronicle

effects.log: Under the last entry, in your own hand, you write: and it was not an omen; it was a friend. You do not know why you wrote it. You do not cross it out.

events.text: A lord's hunters come through your district with a cart, and in the cart is something nobody can name: a roe deer, perhaps, but scaled, with a broken foreleg. The omen-readers argue. Your sleeve is already wet.

choices.text: Buy it from the hunters, whatever they ask (30 taels)

effects.log: Thirty taels. You splint the leg yourself, badly, and keep it in your barn all winter. In spring it walks out on four legs and does not look back, and you sit on the barn floor and weep with relief, for this one, and for one you never saw.

choices.text: Stand in the road in front of the cart

ok.log: You stand in the road and will not move, and the hunters, uneasy, finally tip the creature out on the verge and drive on. It is only a deer with odd markings, you tell yourself, splinting its leg. You do not believe yourself.

fail.log: They knock you down and drive on. But the creature in the cart turned its head to look at you as it passed, and you will never forget that it looked grateful. (-10 health)

events.text: In the ruins of a conqueror's palace, long fallen, there is a cage of gold in the treasury that nobody has ever managed to carry off: it is too heavy, they say, or it will not leave. On the walls the conqueror's war banners rot, each one painted with a gentle five-coloured beast. Tied to one bar of the cage is a torn ribbon.

choices.text: Untie the torn ribbon

effects.log: Your fingers know the knot. It comes away easily, as if it had only been waiting for someone to bother. Behind you, someone in the ruined hall sighs, a long breath like a beast lying down at last. When you turn, there is nobody.

choices.text: Tear down the banners

effects.log: You pull them down one by one and they fall to dust. Every one of them was a lie: a war under the sign of a creature that never fought. When the last is down, the hall feels clean, and the gold of the cage looks, suddenly, cheap.

events.text: A rising warlord, very charming, has begun painting a gentle five-coloured beast on banners and saying it came to bless the warlord's cause. Crowds are cheering. You feel the bars of a cage close round your chest.

choices.text: Tell the crowds about the cage in the ruined palace

ok.log: You tell it everywhere: the conqueror, the cage, the torn ribbon, the lie on the banners. Slowly, the crowds stop cheering at the banners and start asking questions. The warlord's cause does not survive the questions.

fail.log: The warlord's people beat you in the street for it. But the story is told now, and people repeat it, and in a few years the banners with the gentle beast on them are a joke in every tavern. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go and paint a cage onto every banner you can reach

effects.log: You climb up at night with a pot of black paint and paint bars across the gentle beast on every banner you can reach. The warlord's soldiers wake to banners of a beast in a cage. Some of them laugh. Some of them do not, and desert.

events.text: In a warlord family's ancestral shrine, the great treasure is a horn tip of white bone on dark velvet, from the war-beast the founder rode, they say, at the head of every army: magnificent, terrible, a beast that the armies followed like a banner. When you look at it, your forehead aches and you feel very, very tired.

choices.text: Ask the family if you may hold it

effects.log: They let you, curious. The bone is cold. You feel, for a breath, the weight of a saddle, the smell of a thousand battles, and under all of it, very small and far down, a meadow of grass where something once walked without bending anything. You give it back, and your hands shake.

choices.text: Turn and walk out

effects.log: You walk out without a word. That night you dream of soft flesh on the tip of a horn, and wake with your hand pressed to your own forehead, as if to keep something there from hardening.

events.text: You have been winning fights for years, and you are good at it, and lately your heart goes hard each time, the way bone shows when flesh wears thin. Someone has noticed and asked you to lead their war band.

choices.text: Refuse, and go and mend something you broke

effects.log: You refuse. You go back to the village where you broke a man's arm in a quarrel twenty years ago, and bring the family rice, and stay to rebuild the wall your fight knocked down. It takes a summer. Your heart is soft again by autumn.

choices.text: Lead them

effects.log: You lead them. They follow you like an army follows a horn. You win. You do not feel anything at all about it, which is how you know.

events.text: On a night journey along the cliff path above the rapids, you see a streak of light go up from a stone before a cave, into the sky, and not come back. And from inside the cave, very small, comes a sound like a newborn foal crying for something that has just left.

choices.text: Go to the cave mouth and sit just outside it

effects.log: You sit outside till dawn, so that it will not be alone, not going in, not looking. At first light a small soft nose pushes out between the vines and smells you and goes back in. You have the strongest feeling that it remembers everything, and that you were part of it, and that it is glad you are here this time.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of dew and go on

effects.log: You fill a bowl from the wet leaves and set it at the cave mouth and walk on. You never come back that way. But all your life, on the night of that same moon, you wake and listen for rapids.

events.text: Years later, in your village, a young beast you half recognise comes to the brushwood gate at dusk, grey-gold, with a bud of horn, and stands very still, because an ant road crosses the threshold. It looks at you as if it had known you in another life and were deciding whether to say so.

choices.text: Kneel and wait for the ants with it

effects.log: You kneel. The ants go by. It sets its hoof down at last on the bare stone, carefully, and looks at you, and you both know, and neither of you says it. It goes. It will be back, you think, at a birth, with a ribbon. You hope you live to see it.

choices.text: Tell it: you are doing it right this time too

effects.log: You say it aloud, feeling foolish. It lays its ears back, very slightly, and blows warm breath on your hands. You do not know what it did wrong last time. You know it is doing it right now.

events.text: You are old in the valley of sword fences, and the children have started asking where swords came from, and what they were for. None of them has ever seen one used.

choices.text: Tell them the truth, plainly

effects.log: You tell them: what a sword is for. They listen with puzzled faces, the way you would listen to a story about people who ate stones. One of them says, "But why?" You find you cannot answer. That, you think, is the whole of the Great Peace: a child who cannot understand the question.

choices.text: Tell them they hold up beans

effects.log: "They hold up beans," you say. The children accept this. It is true, after all. You laugh for a long time on your porch, alone, and something in the dawn sky over the valley seems to laugh with you.

events.text: A poet you meet on the road has just come from the pavilion above the rapids, and recites you a new poem about the stone with two sets of hoofprints: the beast went, and did not return; where has it gone?

choices.text: Tell the poet where it went

effects.log: "Up," you say, "with someone who trusted it, so that they would not go alone." The poet stares at you, and writes it down, and it becomes the last line of the poem. You never tell the poet how you knew.

choices.text: Let the question stand

effects.log: You say nothing. Some questions are better than their answers. The poet goes on to the next town reciting it, and it goes round the country, and every child who learns it looks up at the sky for a moment, which is perhaps the point.

events.text: You are teaching, late in life, and a student asks why the old chronicle stops where it does, at a hunt in the west. "Did the writer die?" the student asks. "Did he run out of paper?"

choices.text: Say: he saw a friend in a cart, and could not go on

effects.log: The class goes quiet. You did not mean to say it like that. A student at the back, a gentle one, puts a sleeve to their face, and you see that the sleeve is wet, and you think: so it goes on. So it does not end.

choices.text: Say: some stories end where they break

effects.log: "Some stories end where they break," you say, "and the next writer must decide whether to mend them." The students take that as homework. One of them writes a new chapter in which the beast is let go. It is the best essay you have ever marked.

events.text: Two kings have come to sign a peace at the edge of the unmown field, as their ancestors did, and they have asked for a witness from among the common people. They chose you, because you are always at the field's edge.

choices.text: Witness, and say one thing

effects.log: When they have signed you say: "Something lay down here so that you could stand there." Both kings look at the grass. Neither speaks. They walk away from the field together, slowly, like two people leaving a grave.

choices.text: Witness, and say nothing

effects.log: You sign your mark and say nothing. The field says it for you: the wind goes over the tall grass and every blade bends and rises again, and nothing is broken.

events.text: You are dying, old, in your own bed. As your eyes close you see, not your ceiling, but stone, painted with lotus and immortals, and something gentle among them, faded nearly to nothing, looking down at you as at a sleeper it has promised to watch.

choices.text: Let it watch

effects.log: You let it. You are not afraid. You sleep, and it watches, and it seems to you that it will go on watching for a very long time, as long as it takes, and that this was always what it was for.

choices.text: Ask it to rest now

effects.log: "You can rest," you whisper. The faded thing on the stone seems to lower its head, and the last of its colour goes out, gently, like a lamp turned down by someone who loves the sleeper. You wake in the morning, to your surprise, and live three more good years.

events.text: In your old age you are asked by a young ruler, a good one by all reports, whether it would be wise to have the gentle five-coloured beast painted on the royal banners, to show the people the reign is blessed.

choices.text: Tell the ruler about the gold cage in the ruins

effects.log: You tell it all. The ruler listens, and then says, "Then I will paint nothing on my banners, and if it ever comes, it will come to the people, not to me." You go home thinking that perhaps the age is turning.

choices.text: Say: paint it walking away

effects.log: "Paint it walking away," you say, "into the trees. So you remember it does not belong to you." The ruler does. It is a strange banner. People love it.
